title: Acute coronary syndromes – Definition
content: Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) is an umbrella term covering a number of acute presentations of ischaemic heart disease.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Included presentations
content: ACS includes ST elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI), and unstable angina.

title: Unstable angina – Definition and diagnosis
content: Unstable angina is considered present in patients with ischaemic symptoms suggestive of ACS and no elevation in troponins, with or without ECG changes indicative of ischaemia.

title: Unstable angina and NSTEMI – Initial indistinguishability
content: Because troponin elevation may take hours to appear, unstable angina may be initially indistinguishable from NSTEMI and is treated the same until troponin results are available.

title: Ischaemic heart disease – Synonyms
content: Ischaemic heart disease is synonymous with coronary heart disease and coronary artery disease.

title: Ischaemic heart disease – Pathophysiology overview
content: Ischaemic heart disease describes the gradual buildup of fatty plaques within the walls of coronary arteries.

title: Ischaemic heart disease – Consequences of plaque buildup
content: Plaque buildup causes gradual narrowing of coronary arteries leading to reduced blood and oxygen supply to myocardium during increased demand, causing angina.

title: Ischaemic heart disease – Risk of plaque rupture
content: Fatty plaques in the coronary artery endothelium may rupture suddenly, causing artery occlusion and complete loss of blood and oxygen supply to myocardium.

title: Ischaemic heart disease – Unmodifiable risk factors
content: Unmodifiable risk factors for ischaemic heart disease include increasing age, male gender, and family history.

title: Ischaemic heart disease – Modifiable risk factors
content: Modifiable risk factors for ischaemic heart disease include smoking, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, and obesity.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Chest pain location
content: Chest pain in acute coronary syndromes is classically located on the left side of the chest.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Chest pain radiation
content: Chest pain in acute coronary syndromes may radiate to the left arm or neck.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Atypical chest pain presentation
content: Chest pain may not always be present in acute coronary syndromes; elderly, diabetic, or female patients are more likely to have atypical presentations.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Dyspnoea
content: Dyspnoea is a clinical feature of acute coronary syndromes.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Nausea and vomiting
content: Nausea and vomiting can occur as clinical features in acute coronary syndromes.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Sweating
content: Sweating is a common clinical feature of acute coronary syndromes.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Palpitations
content: Palpitations may be experienced as a clinical feature in acute coronary syndromes.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Definition
content: Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) is a common and important medical presentation involving a spectrum of conditions caused by acute myocardial ischemia.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Classification
content: ACS is classified into ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), non ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI), and unstable angina.

title: ST-elevation myocardial infarction – Definition
content: STEMI is defined by ST-segment elevation on ECG and elevated biomarkers of myocardial damage.

title: Non ST-elevation myocardial infarction – Definition
content: NSTEMI is characterized by ECG changes without ST-segment elevation and elevated biomarkers of myocardial damage.

title: Unstable angina – Definition
content: Unstable angina is a form of ACS characterized by ischemic chest pain without elevated biomarkers of myocardial damage.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Initial management grouping
content: NICE guidelines group ACS patients into two management categories: STEMI and NSTEMI/unstable angina.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Aspirin initial therapy
content: Aspirin 300 mg is recommended as initial drug therapy for all patients with suspected ACS.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Oxygen therapy indication
content: Oxygen should be administered only if the patient has oxygen saturations below 94%, according to British Thoracic Society guidelines.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Morphine use criteria
content: Morphine should be given only to patients with severe chest pain; routine intravenous morphine use is no longer recommended due to potential adverse outcomes.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Nitrate administration
content: Nitrates can be administered sublingually or intravenously for ongoing chest pain or hypertension but should be used cautiously in hypotensive patients.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – STEMI ECG diagnostic criteria
content: STEMI diagnosis requires clinical symptoms consistent with ACS lasting ≥ 20 minutes and persistent ST elevation > 20 minutes in at least two contiguous leads.

title: ST-elevation myocardial infarction – ST elevation threshold in leads V2-V3
content: ST elevation of ≥ 2.5 mm (2.5 small squares) in leads V2-V3 is diagnostic for STEMI in appropriate clinical context.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Prognostic model source
content: The 2006 Global Registry of Acute Coronary Events (GRACE) study was used to derive regression models predicting in-hospital and post-discharge death in patients with acute coronary syndrome.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Age as poor prognostic factor
content: Advanced age is associated with a poorer prognosis in patients with acute coronary syndrome.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Heart failure history as poor prognostic factor
content: Development or history of heart failure predicts worse outcomes in acute coronary syndrome patients.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Peripheral vascular disease as poor prognostic factor
content: Presence of peripheral vascular disease is associated with a poorer prognosis in acute coronary syndrome.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Reduced systolic blood pressure as poor prognostic factor
content: Lower systolic blood pressure at presentation predicts worse outcomes in acute coronary syndrome patients.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Killip classification system
content: The Killip classification stratifies risk after myocardial infarction based on clinical signs of heart failure.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Killip class I features and mortality
content: Killip class I is defined by no clinical signs of heart failure and is associated with a 6% 30-day mortality.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Killip class II features and mortality
content: Killip class II is characterized by lung crackles and S3 heart sound, with a 17% 30-day mortality.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Killip class III features and mortality
content: Killip class III involves frank pulmonary oedema and carries a 38% 30-day mortality risk.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Killip class IV features and mortality
content: Killip class IV is defined by cardiogenic shock and is associated with an 81% 30-day mortality.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Initial serum creatinine concentration as poor prognostic factor
content: Elevated initial serum creatinine concentration predicts worse prognosis in acute coronary syndrome patients.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Elevated initial cardiac markers as poor prognostic factor
content: Elevated initial cardiac biomarkers indicate a worse prognosis in patients with acute coronary syndrome.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Cardiac arrest on admission as poor prognostic factor
content: Cardiac arrest occurring on admission is associated with a poor prognosis in acute coronary syndrome patients.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – ST segment deviation as poor prognostic factor
content: ST segment deviation on ECG at presentation predicts worse outcomes in acute coronary syndrome.

title: Adenosine – Definition and Clinical Use
content: Adenosine is a medication most commonly used to terminate supraventricular tachycardias.

title: Adenosine – Mechanism of Action
content: Adenosine acts as an agonist of the A1 receptor in the atrioventricular (AV) node, causing transient heart block by inhibiting adenylyl cyclase, reducing cAMP, and causing hyperpolarization through increased outward potassium flux.

title: Adenosine – Pharmacokinetics
content: Adenosine has a very short half-life of approximately 8 to 10 seconds.

title: Adenosine – Administration Considerations
content: Due to its short half-life, adenosine should ideally be infused via a large-calibre cannula to ensure rapid delivery.

title: Adenosine – Drug Interactions
content: The effects of adenosine are enhanced by dipyridamole and blocked by theophyllines.

title: Adenosine – Contraindications
content: Adenosine should be avoided in patients with asthma due to the risk of bronchospasm.

title: Adenosine – Adverse Effect: Chest Pain
content: Adenosine administration can cause chest pain as an adverse effect.

title: Adenosine – Adverse Effect: Bronchospasm
content: Adenosine can cause bronchospasm as an adverse effect, particularly in susceptible individuals.

title: Adenosine – Adverse Effect: Transient Flushing
content: Transient flushing is a common adverse effect following adenosine administration.

title: Adenosine – Risk in Wolff-Parkinson-White Syndrome
content: Adenosine can enhance conduction down accessory pathways, potentially increasing ventricular rate in patients with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.

title: Adrenaline – Definition
content: Adrenaline is a sympathomimetic amine with both alpha and beta adrenergic stimulating properties.

title: Adrenaline – Indications
content: Adrenaline is indicated for the treatment of anaphylaxis and cardiac arrest.

title: Adrenaline – Adult Life Support Dose for Anaphylaxis
content: The recommended adult dose of adrenaline for anaphylaxis is 0.5 ml of 1:1,000 concentration administered intramuscularly (IM).

title: Adrenaline – Adult Life Support Dose for Cardiac Arrest
content: The recommended adult dose of adrenaline for cardiac arrest is 10 ml of 1:10,000 concentration intravenously (IV) or alternatively 1 ml of 1:1,000 concentration IV.

title: Adrenaline – Management of Accidental Injection
content: Accidental injection of adrenaline causing digital ischaemia is managed by local infiltration of phentolamine.

title: Adrenaline – Background Physiology
content: Adrenaline is responsible for the fight or flight response and is released by the adrenal glands.

title: Adrenaline – Receptor Targets
content: Adrenaline acts on alpha-1, alpha-2, beta-1, and beta-2 adrenergic receptors.

title: Adrenaline – Vascular Effects on Skeletal Muscle
content: Adrenaline acts on beta-2 receptors in skeletal muscle vessels causing vasodilation.

title: Adrenaline – Cardiovascular Effects
content: Adrenaline increases cardiac output and total peripheral resistance.

title: Adrenaline – Vasoconstriction Effects
content: Adrenaline causes vasoconstriction in the skin and kidneys, resulting in a narrow pulse pressure.

title: Adrenaline – Actions on Alpha Adrenergic Receptors: Insulin Secretion
content: Adrenaline inhibits insulin secretion by the pancreas via alpha adrenergic receptor stimulation.

title: Adrenaline – Actions on Alpha Adrenergic Receptors: Glycogenolysis
content: Adrenaline stimulates glycogenolysis in the liver and muscle via alpha adrenergic receptor activation.

title: Adrenaline – Actions on Alpha Adrenergic Receptors: Glycolysis
content: Adrenaline stimulates glycolysis in muscle via alpha adrenergic receptor activation.

title: Adrenaline – Actions on Beta Adrenergic Receptors: Glucagon Secretion
content: Adrenaline stimulates glucagon secretion in the pancreas via beta adrenergic receptor activation.

title: Adrenaline – Actions on Beta Adrenergic Receptors: ACTH Stimulation
content: Adrenaline stimulates adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) secretion via beta adrenergic receptor activation.

title: Adrenaline – Actions on Beta Adrenergic Receptors: Lipolysis
content: Adrenaline stimulates lipolysis in adipose tissue via beta adrenergic receptor activation.

title: Amiodarone – Definition
content: Amiodarone is a class III antiarrhythmic agent used in the treatment of atrial, nodal, and ventricular tachycardias.

title: Amiodarone – Mechanism of action
content: Amiodarone primarily blocks potassium channels, inhibiting repolarisation and prolonging the cardiac action potential; it also blocks sodium channels, exhibiting a class I antiarrhythmic effect.

title: Amiodarone – Half-life and dosing implications
content: Amiodarone has a very long half-life ranging from 20 to 100 days, necessitating the use of loading doses to achieve therapeutic levels.

title: Amiodarone – Administration route considerations
content: Amiodarone should ideally be administered via central veins to reduce the risk of thrombophlebitis.

title: Amiodarone – Proarrhythmic effects
content: Amiodarone can cause proarrhythmic effects by lengthening the QT interval, which may predispose to arrhythmias.

title: Amiodarone – Drug interactions
content: Amiodarone is a cytochrome P450 inhibitor and can decrease the metabolism of concurrently used drugs such as warfarin.

title: Amiodarone – Baseline monitoring before treatment
content: Before starting amiodarone, thyroid function tests (TFT), liver function tests (LFT), urea and electrolytes (U&E), and chest X-ray (CXR) should be performed.

title: Amiodarone – Ongoing monitoring during treatment
content: During amiodarone therapy, thyroid function tests and liver function tests should be repeated every 6 months.

title: Amiodarone – Thyroid dysfunction adverse effects
content: Amiodarone can cause thyroid dysfunction, including both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism.

title: Amiodarone – Corneal deposits adverse effect
content: Long-term use of amiodarone may lead to corneal deposits.

title: Amiodarone – Pulmonary toxicity adverse effects
content: Amiodarone can cause pulmonary fibrosis and pneumonitis as long-term adverse effects.

title: Amiodarone – Hepatic toxicity adverse effects
content: Amiodarone may cause liver fibrosis and hepatitis as adverse effects.

title: Amiodarone – Neuromuscular adverse effects
content: Amiodarone use can lead to peripheral neuropathy and myopathy.

title: Amiodarone – Photosensitivity adverse effect
content: Amiodarone can cause photosensitivity reactions in patients.

title: Amiodarone – Skin discoloration adverse effect
content: Chronic amiodarone use may cause a 'slate-grey' skin discoloration.

title: Amiodarone – Injection site adverse effects
content: Amiodarone administration can cause thrombophlebitis and other injection site reactions.

title: Amiodarone – Bradycardia adverse effect
content: Amiodarone therapy can cause bradycardia as an adverse effect.

title: Amiodarone – QT interval prolongation adverse effect
content: Amiodarone lengthens the QT interval, which can predispose to arrhythmias.

title: Angina pectoris – Overview of management
content: Management of stable angina includes lifestyle changes, medication, percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), and surgery.

title: Angina pectoris – NICE guidelines for stable angina management
content: NICE guidelines published in 2011 provide recommendations for the management of stable angina.

title: Angina pectoris – Aspirin and statin use
content: All patients with stable angina should receive aspirin and a statin unless contraindicated.

title: Angina pectoris – Use of sublingual glyceryl trinitrate
content: Sublingual glyceryl trinitrate is used to abort angina attacks.

title: Angina pectoris – First-line antianginal therapy choice
content: NICE recommends using either a beta-blocker or a calcium channel blocker first-line based on comorbidities, contraindications, and patient preference.

title: Angina pectoris – Calcium channel blocker monotherapy selection
content: If a calcium channel blocker is used as monotherapy, a rate-limiting agent such as verapamil or diltiazem should be chosen.

title: Angina pectoris – Combination therapy with beta-blocker and calcium channel blocker
content: When combining with a beta-blocker, use a longer-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker such as amlodipine or modified-release nifedipine.

title: Angina pectoris – Contraindication of beta-blockers with verapamil
content: Beta-blockers should not be prescribed concurrently with verapamil due to the risk of complete heart block.

title: Angina pectoris – Dose escalation for poor response to initial treatment
content: If there is a poor response to initial treatment, medication should be increased to the maximum tolerated dose, e.g., atenolol up to 100 mg once daily.

title: Angina pectoris – Addition of second-line agent after monotherapy failure
content: If a patient remains symptomatic after monotherapy with a beta-blocker, add a calcium channel blocker, and vice versa.

title: Angina pectoris – Alternative drugs when combination therapy not tolerated
content: If a patient on monotherapy cannot tolerate adding a calcium channel blocker or beta-blocker, consider long-acting nitrates, ivabradine, nicorandil, or ranolazine.

title: Angina pectoris – Addition of third drug during PCI or CABG assessment
content: If a patient is taking both a beta-blocker and a calcium channel blocker, only add a third drug while awaiting assessment for PCI or coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG).

title: Angina pectoris – Nitrate tolerance development
content: Many patients taking nitrates develop tolerance, leading to reduced efficacy of the medication.

title: Angina pectoris – Asymmetric dosing to prevent nitrate tolerance
content: Patients taking standard-release isosorbide mononitrate should use an asymmetric dosing interval to maintain a daily nitrate-free period of 10-14 hours to minimize nitrate tolerance.

title: Angina pectoris – Modified-release isosorbide mononitrate and nitrate tolerance
content: Once-daily modified-release isosorbide mononitrate does not cause nitrate tolerance due to its dosing profile.

title: Angiotensin II receptor blockers – Definition
content: Angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs) are medications that block the effects of angiotensin II at the AT1 receptor.

title: Angiotensin II receptor blockers – Indication after ACE inhibitor intolerance
content: ARBs are generally used in patients who have not tolerated ACE inhibitors, usually due to the development of a cough.

title: Angiotensin II receptor blockers – Examples
content: Examples of ARBs include candesartan, losartan, and irbesartan.

title: Angiotensin II receptor blockers – Caution in renovascular disease
content: ARBs should be used with caution in patients with renovascular disease, similar to ACE inhibitors.

title: Angiotensin II receptor blockers – Side effects
content: Common side effects of ARBs include hypotension and hyperkalaemia.

title: Angiotensin II receptor blockers – Mechanism of action
content: ARBs block the effects of angiotensin II at the AT1 receptor, preventing vasoconstriction and aldosterone secretion.

title: Angiotensin II receptor blockers – Evidence in diabetic nephropathy
content: ARBs have been shown to reduce progression of renal disease in patients with diabetic nephropathy.

title: Losartan – Evidence in cardiovascular mortality reduction
content: Losartan has evidence supporting reduction of cerebrovascular accident (CVA) and ischaemic heart disease (IHD) mortality in hypertensive patients.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – First-line antiplatelet therapy
content: For medically treated acute coronary syndrome, first-line antiplatelet therapy consists of lifelong aspirin combined with ticagrelor for 12 months.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Second-line antiplatelet therapy
content: If aspirin is contraindicated in medically treated acute coronary syndrome, lifelong clopidogrel is recommended as second-line antiplatelet therapy.

title: Percutaneous coronary intervention – First-line antiplatelet therapy
content: Following percutaneous coronary intervention, first-line antiplatelet therapy includes lifelong aspirin combined with prasugrel or ticagrelor for 12 months.

title: Percutaneous coronary intervention – Second-line antiplatelet therapy
content: If aspirin is contraindicated after percutaneous coronary intervention, lifelong clopidogrel is recommended as second-line antiplatelet therapy.

title: Transient ischaemic attack – First-line antiplatelet therapy
content: Clopidogrel lifelong is the first-line antiplatelet therapy for patients with transient ischaemic attack.

title: Transient ischaemic attack – Second-line antiplatelet therapy
content: If clopidogrel is not used, aspirin combined with dipyridamole lifelong is recommended as second-line antiplatelet therapy for transient ischaemic attack.

title: Ischaemic stroke – First-line antiplatelet therapy
content: Lifelong clopidogrel is the first-line antiplatelet therapy for ischaemic stroke.

title: Ischaemic stroke – Second-line antiplatelet therapy
content: If clopidogrel is not used, aspirin combined with dipyridamole lifelong is recommended as second-line antiplatelet therapy for ischaemic stroke.

title: Peripheral arterial disease – First-line antiplatelet therapy
content: Clopidogrel lifelong is the first-line antiplatelet therapy for peripheral arterial disease.

title: Peripheral arterial disease – Second-line antiplatelet therapy
content: Aspirin lifelong is recommended as second-line antiplatelet therapy for peripheral arterial disease.

title: Aortic regurgitation – Definition
content: Aortic regurgitation (AR) is the leaking of the aortic valve of the heart that causes blood to flow in the reverse direction during ventricular diastole.

title: Aortic regurgitation – Pathophysiology
content: Aortic regurgitation occurs due to leaking of the aortic valve causing reverse blood flow into the left ventricle during ventricular diastole.

title: Aortic regurgitation – Causes due to valve disease (chronic)
content: Chronic causes of aortic regurgitation due to valve disease include rheumatic fever, calcific valve disease, connective tissue diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus, and bicuspid aortic valve.

title: Aortic regurgitation – Causes due to aortic root disease (chronic)
content: Chronic causes of aortic regurgitation due to aortic root disease include bicuspid aortic valve, spondylarthropathies such as ankylosing spondylitis, hypertension, syphilis, Marfan's syndrome, and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

title: Aortic regurgitation – Causes due to valve disease (acute)
content: Acute causes of aortic regurgitation due to valve disease include infective endocarditis.

title: Aortic regurgitation – Causes due to aortic root disease (acute)
content: Acute causes of aortic regurgitation due to aortic root disease include aortic dissection.

title: Aortic regurgitation – Clinical feature: Early diastolic murmur
content: Aortic regurgitation presents with an early diastolic murmur whose intensity is increased by the handgrip manoeuvre.

title: Aortic regurgitation – Clinical feature: Collapsing pulse
content: A collapsing pulse is a clinical feature of aortic regurgitation.

title: Aortic regurgitation – Clinical feature: Wide pulse pressure
content: Wide pulse pressure is a clinical feature of aortic regurgitation.

title: Aortic regurgitation – Clinical feature: Quincke's sign
content: Quincke's sign, which is nailbed pulsation, is a clinical feature of aortic regurgitation.

title: Aortic regurgitation – Clinical feature: De Musset's sign
content: De Musset's sign, which is head bobbing, is a clinical feature of aortic regurgitation.

title: Aortic regurgitation – Clinical feature: Austin-Flint murmur
content: A mid-diastolic Austin-Flint murmur occurs in severe aortic regurgitation due to partial closure of the anterior mitral valve cusps caused by regurgitation streams.

title: Aortic regurgitation – Investigation
content: Suspected aortic regurgitation should be investigated with echocardiography.

title: Aortic regurgitation – Management: Medical
content: Medical management of aortic regurgitation includes treatment of any associated heart failure.

title: Aortic regurgitation – Management: Surgical indications
content: Surgical aortic valve replacement is indicated in symptomatic patients with severe aortic regurgitation and in asymptomatic patients with severe aortic regurgitation who have left ventricular systolic dysfunction.

title: Aspirin – Mechanism of action
content: Aspirin blocks the action of cyclooxygenase-1 and cyclooxygenase-2 enzymes, which are responsible for the synthesis of prostaglandins, prostacyclin, and thromboxane.

title: Aspirin – Effect on platelet aggregation
content: By blocking thromboxane A2 formation in platelets, aspirin reduces platelet aggregation, which helps prevent thrombosis in cardiovascular disease.

title: Aspirin – Use in secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease
content: Low-dose aspirin has been widely used for secondary prevention in patients with established cardiovascular disease unless contraindicated.

title: Aspirin – Changes in guidelines after 2010 technology appraisal of clopidogrel
content: Following the 2010 technology appraisal of clopidogrel, aspirin is no longer universally recommended for all patients with established cardiovascular disease.

title: Aspirin – Role in primary prevention of cardiovascular disease
content: Recent trials (Aspirin for Asymptomatic Atherosclerosis and Antithrombotic Trialists Collaboration) have questioned the benefit of aspirin in primary prevention of cardiovascular disease.

title: Aspirin – Regulatory status for primary prevention
content: The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) issued a drug safety update in January 2010 stating aspirin is not licensed for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease.

title: Aspirin – Current guideline recommendation for ischaemic heart disease
content: Aspirin is recommended as first-line antiplatelet therapy for patients with ischaemic heart disease.

title: Aspirin – Drug interactions
content: Aspirin potentiates the effects of oral hypoglycaemics, warfarin, and steroids.

title: Aspirin – Contraindication in children under 16 years
content: Aspirin should not be used in children under 16 years due to the risk of Reye's syndrome, except in Kawasaki disease where benefits outweigh risks.

title: Clopidogrel – Guideline recommendation after ischaemic stroke and peripheral arterial disease
content: NICE recommends clopidogrel as first-line antiplatelet therapy following ischaemic stroke and for peripheral arterial disease, replacing aspirin.

title: Transient ischaemic attacks (TIAs) – Antiplatelet therapy guideline complexity
content: For TIAs, Royal College of Physicians guidelines support clopidogrel use, whereas older NICE guidelines recommend aspirin plus dipyridamole; the RCP considers the older NICE position illogical.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Need for anticoagulation
content: Anticoagulation should be considered in patients with any history of atrial fibrillation, including symptomatic or asymptomatic paroxysmal, persistent, or permanent AF, atrial flutter, and those with a continuing risk of arrhythmia recurrence after cardioversion or catheter ablation.

title: Atrial fibrillation – CHA2DS2-VASc score for anticoagulation decision
content: The CHA2DS2-VASc score is recommended by NICE to determine the need for anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation patients, replacing the older CHADS2 score.

title: Atrial fibrillation – CHA2DS2-VASc score components
content: CHA2DS2-VASc score components and points: Congestive heart failure (1), Hypertension (1), Age ≥75 years (2), Age 65-74 years (1), Diabetes (1), Prior stroke/TIA/thromboembolism (2), Vascular disease (1), Female sex (1).

title: Atrial fibrillation – Anticoagulation strategy based on CHA2DS2-VASc score
content: Anticoagulation recommendations: Score 0 - no treatment; Score 1 - males consider anticoagulation, females no treatment (score 1 due to sex only); Score ≥2 - offer anticoagulation.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Exclusion of valvular heart disease before withholding anticoagulation
content: If CHA2DS2-VASc score suggests no anticoagulation, a transthoracic echocardiogram should be performed to exclude valvular heart disease, which combined with AF is an absolute indication for anticoagulation.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Bleeding risk assessment before anticoagulation
content: Bleeding risk factors include history of falls, old age, alcohol excess, and previous bleeding; however, anticoagulation should not be withheld solely due to age or fall risk.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Use of ORBIT score for bleeding risk assessment
content: NICE recommends formalizing bleeding risk assessment before anticoagulation using the ORBIT score.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Indications for cardioversion
content: Cardioversion in atrial fibrillation is used in two scenarios: as an emergency electrical cardioversion if the patient is haemodynamically unstable, and as an elective procedure (electrical or pharmacological) when a rhythm control strategy is preferred.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Electrical cardioversion synchronization
content: Electrical cardioversion is synchronized to the R wave to avoid delivering a shock during the vulnerable period of cardiac repolarisation, which can induce ventricular fibrillation.

title: Atrial fibrillation – NICE guideline recommendation for rate or rhythm control
content: NICE guidelines recommend offering rate or rhythm control if atrial fibrillation onset is less than 48 hours, and starting rate control if onset is more than 48 hours or uncertain.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Anticoagulation if onset less than 48 hours
content: Patients with atrial fibrillation of less than 48 hours onset should be heparinised; those with risk factors for ischaemic stroke require lifelong oral anticoagulation.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Cardioversion options if onset less than 48 hours
content: For atrial fibrillation less than 48 hours onset, cardioversion may be electrical (DC cardioversion) or pharmacological using amiodarone if structural heart disease is present, or flecainide or amiodarone if absent.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Anticoagulation after electrical cardioversion if onset less than 48 hours
content: If atrial fibrillation is confirmed to be less than 48 hours duration after electrical cardioversion, further anticoagulation is unnecessary.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Anticoagulation before cardioversion if onset more than 48 hours
content: If atrial fibrillation duration exceeds 48 hours, anticoagulation should be administered for at least 3 weeks prior to cardioversion.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Use of transoesophageal echocardiography before cardioversion
content: Transoesophageal echocardiography (TOE) can be performed to exclude left atrial appendage thrombus, allowing immediate heparinisation and cardioversion if no thrombus is detected.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Preferred cardioversion method if onset more than 48 hours
content: NICE recommends electrical cardioversion rather than pharmacological cardioversion for atrial fibrillation lasting more than 48 hours.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Pre-treatment before cardioversion in high risk of failure
content: In patients at high risk of cardioversion failure or atrial fibrillation recurrence, at least 4 weeks of amiodarone or sotalol is recommended prior to electrical cardioversion.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Pharmacological cardioversion guidelines
content: NICE guidelines (2014) and joint AHA, ACC, ESC guidelines (2016) provide recommendations for the pharmacological cardioversion of atrial fibrillation.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Amiodarone efficacy in pharmacological cardioversion
content: Amiodarone is an agent with proven efficacy for pharmacological cardioversion of atrial fibrillation.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Flecainide use in pharmacological cardioversion without structural heart disease
content: Flecainide is effective for pharmacological cardioversion of atrial fibrillation in patients without structural heart disease.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Less commonly used pharmacological cardioversion agents in the UK
content: Quinidine, dofetilide, ibutilide, and propafenone are less commonly used agents for pharmacological cardioversion of atrial fibrillation in the UK.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Beta-blockers are less effective for pharmacological cardioversion
content: Beta-blockers, including sotalol, are less effective agents for pharmacological cardioversion of atrial fibrillation.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Calcium channel blockers are less effective for pharmacological cardioversion
content: Calcium channel blockers are less effective agents for pharmacological cardioversion of atrial fibrillation.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Digoxin is less effective for pharmacological cardioversion
content: Digoxin is a less effective agent for pharmacological cardioversion of atrial fibrillation.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Disopyramide is less effective for pharmacological cardioversion
content: Disopyramide is a less effective agent for pharmacological cardioversion of atrial fibrillation.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Procainamide is less effective for pharmacological cardioversion
content: Procainamide is a less effective agent for pharmacological cardioversion of atrial fibrillation.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Risk factor for ischaemic stroke
content: Atrial fibrillation is a key risk factor for ischaemic stroke.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Importance of recognition post-stroke or TIA
content: Recognising and treating atrial fibrillation after a stroke or transient ischaemic attack (TIA) is crucial for secondary stroke prevention.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Exclusion of haemorrhage before anticoagulation post-stroke or TIA
content: Before starting anticoagulation or antiplatelet therapy following a stroke or TIA, it is essential to exclude cerebral haemorrhage via imaging.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Long-term stroke prevention anticoagulants
content: For long-term stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation, NICE recommends warfarin or direct thrombin or factor Xa inhibitors.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Timing of anticoagulation initiation after TIA
content: Anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation should be started immediately after a TIA once haemorrhage has been excluded by imaging.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Timing of anticoagulation initiation after acute ischaemic stroke
content: In acute ischaemic stroke patients without haemorrhage, anticoagulation therapy should be started after 2 weeks.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Use of antiplatelet therapy between stroke and anticoagulation
content: Antiplatelet therapy should be administered in the period between acute stroke and the initiation of anticoagulation therapy.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Delay of anticoagulation initiation after large cerebral infarction
content: If imaging shows a very large cerebral infarction, initiation of anticoagulation therapy should be delayed beyond the usual 2-week period.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Guideline sources
content: Management of atrial fibrillation is guided by NICE 2021 guidelines and the joint 2012 guidelines from the American Heart Association (AHA), American College of Cardiology (ACC), and European Society of Cardiology (ESC).

title: Atrial fibrillation – Haemodynamic instability indication for electrical cardioversion
content: Patients with atrial fibrillation presenting with signs of haemodynamic instability such as hypotension or heart failure should undergo electrical cardioversion according to peri-arrest tachycardia guidelines.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Acute management based on duration of arrhythmia
content: In haemodynamically stable patients with atrial fibrillation, if the arrhythmia duration is less than 48 hours, either rate or rhythm control can be offered; if 48 hours or more, or if onset is uncertain, rate control is preferred.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Anticoagulation requirement in new-onset AF
content: All patients with new-onset atrial fibrillation require anticoagulation regardless of the time of onset.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Long-term anticoagulation guided by CHA2DS2-VASc score
content: Long-term anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation is determined based on the patient's CHA2DS2-VASc score to assess stroke risk.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Delay of cardioversion with anticoagulation in long-term rhythm control
content: If long-term rhythm control is planned, cardioversion should be delayed until the patient has been on therapeutic anticoagulation for at least 3 weeks.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Rate control as first-line treatment strategy
content: Rate control should be offered as the first-line treatment strategy for atrial fibrillation except in specific patient groups.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Exceptions to first-line rate control strategy
content: Rate control is not first-line in patients whose atrial fibrillation has a reversible cause, those with heart failure primarily caused by AF, new-onset AF less than 48 hours, atrial flutter suitable for ablation, or when rhythm control is clinically preferred.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Beta-blockers for rate control
content: Beta-blockers are commonly used agents for rate control in atrial fibrillation but are contraindicated in patients with asthma.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Calcium channel blockers for rate control
content: Calcium channel blockers are used as rate control agents in atrial fibrillation management.

title: Atrial fibrillation – Digoxin use in rate control
content: Digoxin is no longer considered first-line for rate control in atrial fibrillation due to less effectiveness during exercise and is reserved for patients with minimal physical activity or when other rate-limiting drugs are contraindicated.

title: Atrial flutter – Definition
content: Atrial flutter is a form of supraventricular tachycardia characterised by a succession of rapid atrial depolarisation waves.

title: Atrial flutter – Pathophysiology: Re-entry loop location
content: A large, stable re-entry loop develops in the right atrium in atrial flutter.

title: Atrial flutter – Pathophysiology: Circuit re-excitation
content: The re-entry circuit continuously re-excites atrial tissue in atrial flutter.

title: Atrial flutter – Pathophysiology: Circuit anatomical path
content: The re-entry circuit circles around the tricuspid annulus in atrial flutter.

title: Atrial flutter – Pathophysiology: Cavotricuspid isthmus role
content: The cavotricuspid isthmus, located between the tricuspid valve and inferior vena cava, is a critical slow-conduction zone in atrial flutter.

title: Atrial flutter – Pathophysiology: Anatomical fixation and rhythm regularity
content: Because the re-entry circuit is anatomically fixed, the atrial flutter rhythm is highly regular.

title: Atrial flutter – Pathophysiology: Anatomical dependence and ablation efficacy
content: The anatomical dependence of the re-entry circuit explains why catheter ablation is very effective in atrial flutter.

title: Atrial flutter – ECG findings: Sawtooth pattern
content: The ECG in atrial flutter shows a characteristic 'sawtooth' appearance of flutter waves.

title: Atrial flutter – ECG findings: Atrial and ventricular rates
content: The underlying atrial rate in atrial flutter is often around 300/min; the ventricular rate depends on the degree of AV block, e.g., 2:1 block results in a ventricular rate of 150/min.

title: Atrial flutter – ECG findings: Flutter waves visibility after maneuvers
content: Flutter waves may become visible on ECG following carotid sinus massage or administration of adenosine.

title: Atrial flutter – Management: Similarity to atrial fibrillation treatment
content: Management of atrial flutter is similar to that of atrial fibrillation, although medication may be less effective.

title: Atrial flutter – Management: Sensitivity to cardioversion
content: Atrial flutter is more sensitive to cardioversion than atrial fibrillation, allowing use of lower energy levels.

title: Atrial flutter – Management: Radiofrequency ablation
content: Radiofrequency ablation of the cavotricuspid isthmus is curative for most patients with atrial flutter.

title: Atrial myxoma – Definition
content: Atrial myxoma is the most common primary cardiac tumour.

title: Atrial myxoma – Location prevalence
content: 75% of atrial myxomas occur in the left atrium.

title: Atrial myxoma – Common attachment site
content: Atrial myxomas are most commonly attached to the fossa ovalis region of the interatrial septum.

title: Atrial myxoma – Gender prevalence
content: Atrial myxoma is more common in females.

title: Atrial myxoma – Presentation systemic symptom dyspnoea
content: Dyspnoea is a systemic symptom of atrial myxoma.

title: Atrial myxoma – Presentation systemic symptom fatigue
content: Fatigue is a systemic symptom of atrial myxoma.

title: Atrial myxoma – Presentation systemic symptom weight loss
content: Weight loss is a systemic symptom of atrial myxoma.

title: Atrial myxoma – Presentation systemic symptom pyrexia of unknown origin
content: Pyrexia of unknown origin is a systemic symptom of atrial myxoma.

title: Atrial myxoma – Presentation systemic sign clubbing
content: Clubbing is a systemic sign associated with atrial myxoma.

title: Atrial myxoma – Presentation embolic events
content: Atrial myxoma can cause embolic events.

title: Atrial myxoma – Presentation atrial fibrillation
content: Atrial fibrillation can occur in patients with atrial myxoma.

title: Atrial myxoma – Presentation cardiac murmur
content: A mid-diastolic murmur and a 'tumour plop' sound can be heard in atrial myxoma.

title: Atrial myxoma – Investigation echocardiography findings
content: Echocardiography typically shows a pedunculated heterogeneous mass attached to the fossa ovalis region of the interatrial septum in atrial myxoma.

title: Atrial septal defects – Definition
content: Atrial septal defects (ASDs) are congenital heart defects characterized by an opening in the atrial septum, allowing communication between the left and right atria.

title: Atrial septal defects – Epidemiology in adulthood
content: ASDs are the most likely congenital heart defect to be diagnosed in adulthood.

title: Atrial septal defects – Mortality
content: ASDs carry significant mortality, with 50% of patients dying by 50 years of age if untreated.

title: Atrial septal defects – Types
content: Two main types of ASDs are recognized: ostium secundum and ostium primum.

title: Atrial septal defects – Most common type
content: Ostium secundum ASDs are the most common type, accounting for approximately 70% of cases.

title: Atrial septal defects – Clinical feature: Ejection systolic murmur
content: ASDs commonly present with an ejection systolic murmur due to increased flow across the pulmonary valve.

title: Atrial septal defects – Clinical feature: Fixed splitting of S2
content: Fixed splitting of the second heart sound (S2) is a characteristic clinical sign in ASDs.

title: Atrial septal defects – Complication: Paradoxical embolism
content: Emboli may pass from the venous system to the left side of the heart through the ASD, causing stroke.

title: Ostium secundum ASD – Association with Holt-Oram syndrome
content: Ostium secundum ASDs are associated with Holt-Oram syndrome, characterized by triphalangeal thumbs.

title: Ostium secundum ASD – ECG findings
content: Electrocardiogram in ostium secundum ASDs typically shows right bundle branch block (RBBB) with right axis deviation (RAD).

title: Ostium primum ASD – Presentation timing
content: Ostium primum ASDs tend to present earlier in life than ostium secundum defects.

title: Ostium primum ASD – Association with abnormal AV valves
content: Ostium primum ASDs are associated with abnormalities of the atrioventricular valves.

title: Ostium primum ASD – ECG findings
content: Electrocardiogram in ostium primum ASDs typically shows right bundle branch block (RBBB) with left axis deviation (LAD) and a prolonged PR interval.

title: Atrioventricular block – Definition
content: Atrioventricular (AV) block, or heart block, is a condition characterized by impaired electrical conduction between the atria and ventricles.

title: First-degree heart block – Definition
content: First-degree heart block is a type of AV block characterized by a PR interval greater than 0.2 seconds on ECG.

title: First-degree heart block – Clinical features
content: Asymptomatic first-degree heart block is relatively common and does not require treatment.

title: Second-degree heart block type 1 – Definition
content: Second-degree heart block type 1 (Mobitz I, Wenckebach) is characterized by progressive prolongation of the PR interval until a dropped beat occurs.

title: Second-degree heart block type 2 – Definition
content: Second-degree heart block type 2 (Mobitz II) is characterized by a constant PR interval with P waves often not followed by a QRS complex.

title: Third-degree heart block – Definition
content: Third-degree (complete) heart block is characterized by no association between the P waves and QRS complexes on ECG.

title: B-type natriuretic peptide – Definition
content: B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) is a hormone produced mainly by the left ventricular myocardium in response to strain.

title: B-type natriuretic peptide – Pathophysiology of elevation
content: BNP levels rise primarily due to left ventricular strain; causes include heart failure, myocardial ischaemia, and valvular heart disease.

title: B-type natriuretic peptide – Effect of chronic kidney disease on levels
content: Reduced excretion of BNP in patients with chronic kidney disease can cause elevated BNP levels independent of cardiac function.

title: B-type natriuretic peptide – Factors reducing BNP levels
content: Treatment with ACE inhibitors, angiotensin-2 receptor blockers, and diuretics reduces BNP levels.

title: B-type natriuretic peptide – Physiological effects
content: BNP acts as a vasodilator, promotes diuresis and natriuresis, and suppresses sympathetic tone and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.

title: B-type natriuretic peptide – Diagnostic use in acute dyspnoea
content: A BNP concentration below 100 pg/ml makes heart failure unlikely in patients presenting with acute dyspnoea; elevated levels warrant further investigation.

title: B-type natriuretic peptide – NICE recommendation for heart failure diagnosis
content: NICE recommends BNP testing as a helpful tool to rule out a diagnosis of heart failure.

title: B-type natriuretic peptide – Prognostic value in chronic heart failure
content: BNP is an extremely useful marker of prognosis in patients with chronic heart failure.

title: B-type natriuretic peptide – Use in guiding treatment of chronic heart failure
content: Effective treatment of chronic heart failure lowers BNP levels, which can be used to guide therapy.

title: B-type natriuretic peptide – Screening for cardiac dysfunction
content: Screening for cardiac dysfunction using BNP measurement is not currently recommended for the general population.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Definition of Bivalirudin
content: Bivalirudin is a reversible direct thrombin inhibitor used as an anticoagulant.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Use of Bivalirudin in management
content: Bivalirudin is used as an anticoagulant in the management of acute coronary syndrome.

title: Broad complex tachycardia – AV dissociation suggests ventricular tachycardia
content: The presence of atrioventricular (AV) dissociation during broad complex tachycardia suggests ventricular tachycardia rather than supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction.

title: Broad complex tachycardia – Fusion or capture beats indicate ventricular tachycardia
content: The occurrence of fusion or capture beats during broad complex tachycardia is indicative of ventricular tachycardia rather than supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction.

title: Broad complex tachycardia – Positive QRS concordance in chest leads suggests ventricular tachycardia
content: Positive QRS concordance across the chest leads during broad complex tachycardia supports the diagnosis of ventricular tachycardia over supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction.

title: Broad complex tachycardia – Marked left axis deviation suggests ventricular tachycardia
content: Marked left axis deviation on ECG during broad complex tachycardia is a feature suggestive of ventricular tachycardia rather than supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction.

title: Broad complex tachycardia – History of ischaemic heart disease supports ventricular tachycardia diagnosis
content: A history of ischaemic heart disease in a patient presenting with broad complex tachycardia increases the likelihood that the arrhythmia is ventricular tachycardia rather than supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction.

title: Broad complex tachycardia – Lack of response to adenosine suggests ventricular tachycardia
content: Failure of broad complex tachycardia to respond to adenosine administration suggests the arrhythmia is ventricular tachycardia rather than supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction.

title: Broad complex tachycardia – Lack of response to carotid sinus massage suggests ventricular tachycardia
content: Broad complex tachycardia that does not respond to carotid sinus massage is more likely to be ventricular tachycardia than supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction.

title: Broad complex tachycardia – QRS duration greater than 160 ms suggests ventricular tachycardia
content: A QRS complex duration exceeding 160 milliseconds during broad complex tachycardia is a diagnostic feature favoring ventricular tachycardia over supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction.

title: Brugada syndrome – Definition
content: Brugada syndrome is an inherited cardiovascular disease characterized by a risk of sudden cardiac death.

title: Brugada syndrome – Inheritance pattern
content: Brugada syndrome is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion.

title: Brugada syndrome – Epidemiology
content: Brugada syndrome has an estimated prevalence of 1 in 5,000 to 1 in 10,000 individuals and is more common in Asians.

title: Brugada syndrome – Pathophysiology genetic variants
content: A large number of genetic variants exist that cause Brugada syndrome.

title: Brugada syndrome – SCN5A gene mutation
content: Approximately 20-40% of Brugada syndrome cases are caused by mutations in the SCN5A gene, which encodes the myocardial sodium ion channel protein.

title: Brugada syndrome – ECG characteristic ST segment elevation
content: Brugada syndrome ECG shows convex ST segment elevation greater than 2 mm in one or more of leads V1 to V3, followed by a negative T wave.

title: Brugada syndrome – ECG partial right bundle branch block
content: Brugada syndrome ECG may show a partial right bundle branch block pattern.

title: Brugada syndrome – Flecainide or ajmaline challenge test
content: Administration of flecainide or ajmaline can unmask or accentuate ECG changes in Brugada syndrome and is the investigation of choice in suspected cases.

title: Brugada syndrome – Management general measures
content: General management of Brugada syndrome includes prompt treatment of fever and avoidance of excessive alcohol consumption.

title: Brugada syndrome – Avoidance of arrhythmia-precipitating drugs
content: Patients with Brugada syndrome should avoid drugs that may precipitate ventricular arrhythmias, including flecainide, lithium, and tricyclic antidepressants.

title: Brugada syndrome – Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator
content: An implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) is used in the management of Brugada syndrome to prevent sudden cardiac death.

title: Buerger's disease – Definition
content: Buerger's disease, also known as thromboangiitis obliterans, is a vasculitis affecting small and medium-sized blood vessels.

title: Buerger's disease – Pathophysiology
content: Buerger's disease is strongly associated with tobacco smoking, which contributes to inflammation and thrombosis in small and medium-sized vessels.

title: Buerger's disease – Presentation: extremity ischaemia
content: Patients with Buerger's disease commonly present with extremity ischaemia due to vessel inflammation and occlusion.

title: Buerger's disease – Presentation: intermittent claudication
content: Intermittent claudication is a common symptom in Buerger's disease, caused by reduced blood flow during exercise.

title: Buerger's disease – Presentation: ischaemic ulcers
content: Ischaemic ulcers may develop in Buerger's disease due to chronic poor blood supply to the extremities.

title: Buerger's disease – Presentation: superficial thrombophlebitis
content: Superficial thrombophlebitis is a clinical feature of Buerger's disease characterized by inflammation and thrombosis of superficial veins.

title: Buerger's disease – Presentation: Raynaud's phenomenon
content: Raynaud's phenomenon, characterized by episodic digital ischemia and color changes, can be a feature of Buerger's disease.

title: Calcium channel blockers – Definition
content: Calcium channel blockers are medications primarily used in the management of cardiovascular disease by inhibiting voltage-gated calcium channels.

title: Calcium channel blockers – Pathophysiology
content: Voltage-gated calcium channels are present in myocardial cells, conduction system cells, and vascular smooth muscle cells, mediating calcium influx essential for contraction and conduction.

title: Calcium channel blockers – Clinical relevance of tissue selectivity
content: Different types of calcium channel blockers have varying effects on myocardial cells, conduction system cells, and vascular smooth muscle, influencing their clinical uses and side effect profiles.

title: Verapamil – Indications
content: Verapamil is indicated for angina, hypertension, and arrhythmias.

title: Verapamil – Pharmacodynamics
content: Verapamil is highly negatively inotropic, reducing myocardial contractility significantly.

title: Verapamil – Drug interactions
content: Verapamil should not be given with beta-blockers due to the risk of causing heart block.

title: Verapamil – Side effects and cautions
content: Side effects of verapamil include heart failure, constipation, hypotension, bradycardia, and flushing.

title: Diltiazem – Indications
content: Diltiazem is indicated for angina and hypertension.

title: Diltiazem – Pharmacodynamics
content: Diltiazem is less negatively inotropic than verapamil but still requires caution in patients with heart failure or those taking beta-blockers.

title: Diltiazem – Side effects and cautions
content: Side effects of diltiazem include hypotension, bradycardia, heart failure, and ankle swelling.

title: Dihydropyridines (nifedipine, amlodipine, felodipine) – Indications
content: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are indicated for hypertension, angina, and Raynaud's phenomenon.

title: Dihydropyridines – Pharmacodynamics
content: Dihydropyridines primarily affect peripheral vascular smooth muscle more than myocardium, avoiding worsening of heart failure but causing peripheral vasodilation.

title: Dihydropyridines – Side effects and cautions
content: Side effects include flushing, headache, and ankle swelling; shorter-acting agents like nifedipine may cause reflex tachycardia due to peripheral vasodilation.

title: Normal cardiac oxygen saturation levels – Definition
content: Deoxygenated blood returns to the right side of the heart via the superior vena cava (SVC) and inferior vena cava (IVC) with an oxygen saturation of around 70%. The right atrium (RA), right ventricle (RV), and pulmonary artery (PA) normally have oxygen saturation levels of around 70%. The lungs oxygenate the blood to 98-100%, so the left atrium (LA), left ventricle (LV), and aorta have oxygen saturation levels of 98-100%.

title: Atrial septal defect (ASD) – Pathophysiology of oxygen saturation changes
content: In ASD, oxygenated blood from the left atrium (LA) mixes with deoxygenated blood in the right atrium (RA), resulting in intermediate oxygen saturation levels (~85%) in the RA, right ventricle (RV), and pulmonary artery (PA), while the left atrium, left ventricle, and aorta maintain normal saturation (98-100%).

title: Ventricular septal defect (VSD) – Pathophysiology of oxygen saturation changes
content: In VSD, oxygenated blood from the left ventricle (LV) mixes with deoxygenated blood in the right ventricle (RV), causing intermediate oxygen saturation (~85%) in the RV and pulmonary artery (PA). The right atrium (RA) remains at normal deoxygenated saturation (~70%). The left atrium, left ventricle, and aorta maintain normal saturation (98-100%).

title: Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) – Pathophysiology of oxygen saturation changes
content: In PDA, the higher pressure aorta connects to the lower pressure pulmonary artery (PA), causing intermediate oxygen saturation (~85%) only in the pulmonary artery. The right atrium (RA) and right ventricle (RV) maintain normal deoxygenated saturation (~70%), and the left atrium (LA), left ventricle (LV), and aorta have normal oxygen saturation (98-100%).

title: Ventricular septal defect with Eisenmenger's syndrome – Oxygen saturation changes
content: In VSD with Eisenmenger's syndrome, the right ventricle (RV), pulmonary artery (PA), and right atrium (RA) have deoxygenated blood saturation (~70%) due to reversed shunting. The left atrium (LA) maintains normal saturation (~100%), but the left ventricle (LV) and aorta show reduced oxygen saturation (~85%).

title: Patent ductus arteriosus with Eisenmenger's syndrome – Oxygen saturation changes
content: In PDA with Eisenmenger's syndrome, the right atrium (RA), right ventricle (RV), and pulmonary artery (PA) have deoxygenated saturation (~70%) due to reversed shunting. The left atrium (LA) and left ventricle (LV) maintain normal saturation (~100%), but the aorta shows reduced oxygen saturation (~85%).

title: Atrial septal defect with Eisenmenger's syndrome – Oxygen saturation changes
content: In ASD with Eisenmenger's syndrome, the right atrium (RA), right ventricle (RV), and pulmonary artery (PA) have deoxygenated saturation (~70%) due to reversed shunting. The left atrium (LA), left ventricle (LV), and aorta show reduced oxygen saturation (~85%).

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Role of troponin T and I in diagnosis
content: Troponin T and I have largely replaced other cardiac enzymes for diagnosing acute coronary syndromes due to their high sensitivity and specificity.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Myoglobin as earliest rising cardiac marker
content: Myoglobin is the first cardiac marker to rise after myocardial injury, increasing within 1-2 hours.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – CK-MB utility in detecting reinfarction
content: CK-MB is useful for detecting reinfarction because it returns to normal within 2-3 days, unlike troponin T which remains elevated up to 10 days.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Myoglobin timing profile
content: Myoglobin begins to rise 1-2 hours after myocardial injury, peaks at 6-8 hours, and returns to normal within 1-2 days.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – CK-MB timing profile
content: CK-MB begins to rise 2-6 hours after myocardial injury, peaks at 16-20 hours, and returns to normal within 2-3 days.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Creatine kinase (CK) timing profile
content: Creatine kinase (CK) begins to rise 4-8 hours after myocardial injury, peaks at 16-24 hours, and returns to normal within 3-4 days.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Troponin T timing profile
content: Troponin T begins to rise 4-6 hours after myocardial injury, peaks at 12-24 hours, and remains elevated for 7-10 days.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) timing profile
content: AST begins to rise 12-24 hours after myocardial injury, peaks at 36-48 hours, and returns to normal within 3-4 days.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) timing profile
content: LDH begins to rise 24-48 hours after myocardial injury, peaks at 72 hours, and returns to normal within 8-10 days.

title: Cardiac imaging – Non-invasive techniques overview
content: Non-invasive cardiac imaging techniques include MRI, CT, and radionuclide imaging, which have rapidly evolved to allow detailed visualization of cardiac structure and function without invasive procedures.

title: Nuclear imaging – Use of radiotracers in cardiac imaging
content: Nuclear imaging uses radiotracers that are extracted by normal myocardium to assess myocardial perfusion and viability.

title: Nuclear imaging – Thallium as a radiotracer
content: Thallium is a radiotracer used in nuclear cardiac imaging to assess myocardial perfusion by being taken up by normal myocardium.

title: Nuclear imaging – Technetium-99m sestamibi (MIBI) in SPECT scans
content: Technetium-99m sestamibi is a radiotracer used in cardiac Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT) scans to evaluate myocardial perfusion.

title: Nuclear imaging – Fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) in PET scans
content: Fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) is a radiotracer used in Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scans to assess myocardial metabolism and viability.

title: SPECT imaging – Assessment of myocardial perfusion and viability
content: Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT) assesses myocardial perfusion and viability by acquiring images at rest and during stress to identify reversible or fixed ischaemia.

title: SPECT imaging – Stress testing methods
content: Stress images in SPECT are obtained either by exercise or pharmacological agents such as adenosine or dipyridamole to evaluate inducible ischaemia.

title: Cardiac PET imaging – Current role
content: Cardiac Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is predominantly used as a research tool currently and is not widely applied in routine clinical practice.

title: MUGA scan – Definition and purpose
content: Multi Gated Acquisition (MUGA) scan, also known as radionuclide angiography, is a nuclear imaging technique used to evaluate cardiac function, especially left ventricular ejection fraction.

title: MUGA scan – Procedure
content: MUGA scan involves intravenous injection of technetium-99m radionuclide followed by imaging with a gamma camera to assess cardiac function.

title: MUGA scan – Use as stress test
content: MUGA scan can be performed as a stress test to evaluate cardiac function under stress conditions.

title: MUGA scan – Measurement of left ventricular ejection fraction
content: MUGA scan accurately measures left ventricular ejection fraction and is typically used before and after administration of cardiotoxic drugs to monitor cardiac function.

title: Cardiac CT – Role in ischaemic heart disease assessment
content: Cardiac Computed Tomography (CT) is useful in assessing suspected ischaemic heart disease by evaluating coronary artery calcium and lumen anatomy.

title: Cardiac CT – Calcium scoring
content: Calcium scoring quantifies the amount of atherosclerotic plaque calcium in coronary arteries, correlating with the risk of future ischaemic events.

title: Cardiac CT – Contrast-enhanced imaging
content: Contrast-enhanced cardiac CT allows visualization of the coronary artery lumen to detect stenosis or occlusion.

title: Cardiac CT – Combined calcium scoring and contrast-enhanced imaging
content: Combining calcium scoring with contrast-enhanced CT provides a high negative predictive value for excluding ischaemic heart disease.

title: Cardiac tamponade – Definition
content: Cardiac tamponade is characterized by the accumulation of pericardial fluid under pressure.

title: Cardiac tamponade – Beck's triad: Hypotension
content: Hypotension is a classical feature of cardiac tamponade as part of Beck's triad.

title: Cardiac tamponade – Beck's triad: Raised jugular venous pressure
content: Raised jugular venous pressure (JVP) is a classical feature of cardiac tamponade as part of Beck's triad.

title: Cardiac tamponade – Beck's triad: Muffled heart sounds
content: Muffled heart sounds are a classical feature of cardiac tamponade as part of Beck's triad.

title: Cardiac tamponade – Dyspnoea
content: Dyspnoea is a common presenting symptom in cardiac tamponade.

title: Cardiac tamponade – Tachycardia
content: Tachycardia is a common presenting sign in cardiac tamponade.

title: Cardiac tamponade – Absent Y descent on jugular venous pressure
content: An absent Y descent on the jugular venous pressure waveform occurs in cardiac tamponade due to limited right ventricular filling.

title: Cardiac tamponade – Pulsus paradoxus
content: Pulsus paradoxus is an abnormally large drop in blood pressure during inspiration and is a feature of cardiac tamponade.

title: Cardiac tamponade – Kussmaul's sign
content: Kussmaul's sign may be present in cardiac tamponade, but its significance is debated.

title: Cardiac tamponade – ECG electrical alternans
content: Electrical alternans on ECG is a characteristic finding in cardiac tamponade.

title: Cardiac tamponade – Jugular venous pressure comparison with constrictive pericarditis
content: In cardiac tamponade, the Y descent on jugular venous pressure is absent, whereas in constrictive pericarditis both X and Y descents are present.

title: Cardiac tamponade – Pulsus paradoxus comparison with constrictive pericarditis
content: Pulsus paradoxus is present in cardiac tamponade but absent in constrictive pericarditis.

title: Cardiac tamponade – Kussmaul's sign comparison with constrictive pericarditis
content: Kussmaul's sign is rare in cardiac tamponade but present in constrictive pericarditis.

title: Constrictive pericarditis – Characteristic feature: Pericardial calcification on chest X-ray
content: Pericardial calcification on chest X-ray is a characteristic feature of constrictive pericarditis, not seen in cardiac tamponade.

title: Cardiac tamponade – Mnemonic for absent Y descent: TAMponade = TAMpaX
content: The mnemonic 'TAMponade = TAMpaX' is used to remember the absent Y descent in cardiac tamponade jugular venous pressure waveform.

title: Cardiac tamponade – Management: Urgent pericardiocentesis
content: Urgent pericardiocentesis is the primary management for cardiac tamponade to relieve pressure from pericardial fluid accumulation.

title: Cardiomyopathies – Classification update
content: The old classification of dilated, restrictive, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy has been largely abandoned due to high overlap; the latest WHO and American Heart Association classifications reflect this change.

title: Primary cardiomyopathies – Definition
content: Primary cardiomyopathies predominantly involve the heart muscle without an identifiable secondary cause.

title: Genetic cardiomyopathies – Inheritance pattern
content: Genetic primary cardiomyopathies are typically inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.

title: Genetic cardiomyopathies – ICD implantation
content: Implantable cardioverter-defibrillators are often inserted in genetic cardiomyopathies to reduce the incidence of sudden cardiac death.

title: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy – Leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes
content: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy is the leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes.

title: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy – Genetic mutation
content: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy is usually caused by a mutation in the gene encoding the β-myosin heavy chain protein.

title: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy – Echocardiographic findings
content: Echocardiography in hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy shows mitral regurgitation, systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the anterior mitral valve, and asymmetric septal hypertrophy.

title: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia – Pathophysiology
content: In arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia, the right ventricular myocardium is replaced by fatty and fibrofatty tissue.

title: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia – Genetic mutations
content: Approximately 50% of patients with arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia have mutations in genes encoding desmosomal proteins.

title: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia – ECG findings
content: ECG abnormalities in arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia include T wave inversion in leads V1-V3 and an epsilon wave in about 50% of cases, characterized as a terminal notch in the QRS complex.

title: Mixed cardiomyopathies – Definition
content: Mixed cardiomyopathies describe patients with a genetic predisposition to cardiomyopathy triggered by secondary processes, reflecting overlap between primary and secondary causes.

title: Dilated cardiomyopathy – Classic causes
content: Classic causes of dilated cardiomyopathy include alcohol abuse, Coxsackie B virus infection, wet beri beri (thiamine deficiency), and doxorubicin toxicity.

title: Restrictive cardiomyopathy – Classic causes
content: Classic causes of restrictive cardiomyopathy include amyloidosis, post-radiotherapy fibrosis, and Loeffler's endocarditis.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Immediate management with glyceryl trinitrate
content: Glyceryl trinitrate is used in the immediate management of suspected acute coronary syndrome (ACS) to relieve chest pain.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Immediate management with aspirin 300mg
content: Aspirin 300mg should be administered immediately in suspected acute coronary syndrome (ACS) patients; other antiplatelet agents like clopidogrel are not recommended outside hospital.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Oxygen therapy recommendations
content: Oxygen should not be routinely given in suspected ACS; supplemental oxygen is only indicated if oxygen saturation is below 94%, with specific targets for patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Oxygen saturation targets in COPD patients
content: In patients with COPD at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, oxygen therapy aims for SpO2 of 88-92% until blood gas analysis is available.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – ECG use in suspected ACS
content: An ECG should be performed as soon as possible in suspected ACS but should not delay transfer to hospital; a normal ECG does not exclude ACS.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Referral criteria for chest pain within 12 hours and abnormal ECG
content: Patients with current chest pain or chest pain within the last 12 hours and an abnormal ECG require emergency hospital admission.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Referral criteria for chest pain 12-72 hours ago
content: Patients with chest pain occurring 12 to 72 hours prior should be referred to hospital the same day for assessment.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Assessment for chest pain >72 hours ago
content: For chest pain occurring more than 72 hours ago, a full assessment including ECG and troponin measurement should be performed before deciding further management.

title: Stable angina – Definition of typical anginal pain
content: Typical anginal pain is defined by constricting discomfort in the front of the chest or neck, shoulders, jaw, or arms; precipitated by physical exertion; and relieved by rest or glyceryl trinitrate within about 5 minutes.

title: Stable angina – Classification of angina based on symptom features
content: Patients with all three typical angina features have typical angina; those with two features have atypical angina; those with one or none have non-anginal chest pain.

title: Choking – Definition
content: Choking is a life-threatening emergency caused by partial or complete airway obstruction.

title: Choking – Common trigger
content: Episodes of choking often occur whilst eating.

title: Choking – Patient behavior during airway obstruction
content: Patients often clutch their neck during episodes of airway obstruction.

title: Choking – Initial assessment question
content: The first step in suspected choking is to ask the patient 'Are you choking?'.

title: Choking – Mild airway obstruction response to question
content: In mild airway obstruction, the victim can speak and answers 'yes' to the question 'Are you choking?'.

title: Choking – Mild airway obstruction other signs
content: In mild airway obstruction, the victim is able to speak, cough, and breathe.

title: Choking – Severe airway obstruction response to question
content: In severe airway obstruction, the victim is unable to speak and may respond by nodding.

title: Choking – Severe airway obstruction other signs
content: In severe airway obstruction, the victim is unable to breathe, breathing sounds wheezy, attempts at coughing are silent, and the victim may be unconscious.

title: Choking – Management of mild airway obstruction
content: If mild airway obstruction is present, encourage the patient to cough.

title: Choking – Management of severe airway obstruction in conscious patient
content: If severe airway obstruction occurs in a conscious patient, give up to 5 back blows; if unsuccessful, give up to 5 abdominal thrusts; if still unsuccessful, continue the cycle of back blows and abdominal thrusts.

title: Choking – Management of unconscious patient with airway obstruction
content: If the patient with airway obstruction is unconscious, call for an ambulance and start cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR).

title: Chronic heart failure – First-line diagnostic test
content: All patients suspected of chronic heart failure should have an N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) blood test as the first-line investigation, regardless of previous myocardial infarction history.

title: Chronic heart failure – Interpretation of NT-proBNP levels for referral timing
content: If NT-proBNP levels are high (>2000 pg/ml), specialist assessment including transthoracic echocardiography should be arranged within 2 weeks; if levels are raised (400-2000 pg/ml), assessment should be arranged within 6 weeks.

title: Chronic heart failure – Role of serum natriuretic peptides
content: B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) is a hormone produced mainly by the left ventricular myocardium in response to myocardial strain; very high BNP levels are associated with poor prognosis in chronic heart failure.

title: Chronic heart failure – BNP level thresholds
content: BNP levels are classified as high if >400 pg/ml, raised if 100-400 pg/ml, and normal if <100 pg/ml; corresponding NT-proBNP thresholds are high >2000 pg/ml, raised 400-2000 pg/ml, and normal <400 pg/ml.

title: Chronic heart failure – Factors increasing BNP levels
content: Conditions and factors that increase BNP levels include left ventricular hypertrophy, ischaemia, tachycardia, right ventricular overload, hypoxaemia (including pulmonary embolism), glomerular filtration rate <60 ml/min, sepsis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes, age over 70 years, and liver cirrhosis.

title: Chronic heart failure – Factors decreasing BNP levels
content: Factors that decrease BNP levels include obesity and use of medications such as diuretics, ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, angiotensin II receptor blockers, and aldosterone antagonists.

title: Chronic heart failure – Role of loop diuretics
content: Loop diuretics such as furosemide are important for managing fluid overload in chronic heart failure but have not demonstrated long-term mortality reduction.

title: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction – First-line drug treatment
content: The first-line drug treatment for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction includes ACE-inhibitor, beta-blocker, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, and SGLT2-inhibitor.

title: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction – ACE-inhibitor intolerance management
content: If ACE-inhibitors are not tolerated due to cough, switch to angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI); if angioedema develops, switch to angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB).

title: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction – Use of clinical judgement in drug initiation
content: Clinical judgement is recommended when initiating the four first-line medications to avoid starting all simultaneously and to identify adverse drug reactions.

title: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction – Management of persistent symptoms on first-line drugs
content: If symptoms persist despite first-line treatment, switch ACE-inhibitor to angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor such as sacubitril-valsartan after consulting a heart failure specialist.

title: Chronic heart failure – Assessment for iron deficiency
content: Assess iron deficiency by measuring transferrin saturation, ferritin, and haemoglobin in patients with chronic heart failure.

title: Chronic heart failure – Indications for intravenous iron therapy
content: Consider intravenous iron therapy if haemoglobin is less than 150 g/L and transferrin saturation is below 20% or serum ferritin is less than 100 ng/mL after excluding other causes of iron deficiency.

title: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction – First-line drug treatment
content: The first-line drug treatment for heart failure with preserved ejection fraction includes mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and SGLT2-inhibitor.

title: ACE inhibitors, ARNIs, ARBs and MRAs – Monitoring urea and electrolytes
content: Measure urea and electrolytes before starting treatment, 1-2 weeks after initiation, 1-2 weeks after each dose increment, and every 3 to 6 months thereafter.

title: Chronic heart failure – NYHA classification overview
content: The New York Heart Association (NYHA) classification is a system used to classify the severity of chronic heart failure based on symptoms and physical activity limitations.

title: Chronic heart failure – NYHA Class I definition
content: NYHA Class I is defined as no symptoms and no limitation of physical activity; ordinary physical exercise does not cause undue fatigue, dyspnoea, or palpitations.

title: Chronic heart failure – NYHA Class II definition
content: NYHA Class II is characterized by mild symptoms and slight limitation of physical activity; patients are comfortable at rest but ordinary activity results in fatigue, palpitations, or dyspnoea.

title: Chronic heart failure – NYHA Class III definition
content: NYHA Class III involves moderate symptoms and marked limitation of physical activity; patients are comfortable at rest but less than ordinary activity causes symptoms.

title: Chronic heart failure – NYHA Class IV definition
content: NYHA Class IV is defined by severe symptoms; patients are unable to carry out any physical activity without discomfort and have symptoms of heart failure even at rest, with increased discomfort on any physical activity.

title: Clopidogrel – Definition and Drug Class
content: Clopidogrel is an antiplatelet agent belonging to the thienopyridine class of drugs.

title: Clopidogrel – Indications in Cardiovascular Disease
