content: If a person at risk of infective endocarditis is undergoing gastrointestinal or genitourinary procedures at a site with suspected infection and receiving antimicrobial therapy, they should be given antibiotics covering organisms that cause infective endocarditis.

title: Infective endocarditis – guideline differences between NICE and AHA/ESC
content: NICE guidelines do not recommend antibiotic prophylaxis for dental procedures, whereas American Heart Association and European Society of Cardiology guidelines still advocate prophylaxis for high-risk patients undergoing dental procedures.

title: Inhaled foreign body – Definition
content: Inhaled foreign body refers to the entry of an external object into the respiratory tract, commonly occurring in younger children.

title: Inhaled foreign body – Epidemiology
content: Inhaled foreign body typically occurs in younger children.

title: Inhaled foreign body – Presentation timing
content: Presentation of inhaled foreign body is often acute but can sometimes go unnoticed, with up to a third of cases diagnosed after a few days.

title: Inhaled foreign body – Clinical feature: cough
content: Cough is a common clinical feature of inhaled foreign body.

title: Inhaled foreign body – Clinical feature: stridor
content: Stridor is a common clinical feature of inhaled foreign body.

title: Inhaled foreign body – Clinical feature: dyspnoea
content: Dyspnoea is a common clinical feature of inhaled foreign body.

title: Inhaled foreign body – Pathophysiology: location of foreign body
content: Aspirated foreign bodies are most likely to be found in the right main bronchus because it is wider, shorter, and more vertical than the left main bronchus.

title: Palpitations – Definition
content: Palpitations are a common presenting symptom characterized by the sensation of an abnormal or irregular heartbeat.

title: Palpitations – Causes: Arrhythmias
content: Arrhythmias are a possible cause of palpitations, involving abnormal heart rhythms that can be episodic or sustained.

title: Palpitations – Causes: Stress
content: Stress can cause palpitations by increasing sympathetic nervous system activity, leading to heightened awareness of heartbeats.

title: Palpitations – Causes: Increased awareness of normal heartbeat and extrasystoles
content: Increased awareness of normal heartbeat or benign extrasystoles can cause palpitations without underlying pathological arrhythmia.

title: Palpitations – Investigation: 12-lead ECG
content: A 12-lead ECG is a first-line investigation for palpitations that records heart rhythm for a few seconds and may detect underlying abnormalities such as prolonged QT or PR intervals or signs of recent myocardial ischaemia.

title: Palpitations – Investigation: Thyroid function tests
content: Thyroid function tests are performed to detect thyrotoxicosis, which may precipitate atrial fibrillation and other arrhythmias causing palpitations.

title: Palpitations – Investigation: Urea and electrolytes
content: Urea and electrolyte tests are used to identify disturbances such as hypokalemia that may contribute to arrhythmias causing palpitations.

title: Palpitations – Investigation: Full blood count
content: A full blood count is performed to identify hematological abnormalities that may contribute to palpitations.

title: Palpitations – Capturing episodic arrhythmias
content: First-line investigations may be normal in palpitations; capturing episodic arrhythmias requires prolonged monitoring to correlate symptoms with heart rhythm abnormalities.

title: Palpitations – Investigation: Holter monitoring
content: Holter monitoring is a portable, battery-operated device that continuously records ECG from 2-3 leads, usually for 24 hours, to detect episodic arrhythmias in patients with palpitations.

title: Palpitations – Holter monitoring: Patient diary
content: During Holter monitoring, patients keep a diary to record symptomatic palpitations, which is later compared to ECG recordings to correlate symptoms with arrhythmias.

title: Palpitations – Holter monitoring: Report parameters
content: The Holter monitor report summarizes parameters including heart rate, arrhythmias, and ECG waveform changes detected during the monitoring period.

title: Palpitations – Investigation: External loop recorder
content: If Holter monitoring is normal and symptoms persist, an external loop recorder may be used to capture infrequent arrhythmias by recording ECG over extended periods.

title: Palpitations – Investigation: Implantable loop recorder
content: An implantable loop recorder may be used for long-term ECG monitoring to detect rare arrhythmias in patients with ongoing palpitations and normal initial investigations.

title: Isolated systolic hypertension – Definition
content: Isolated systolic hypertension (ISH) is a condition characterized by elevated systolic blood pressure with normal diastolic blood pressure, commonly seen in elderly patients.

title: Isolated systolic hypertension – Epidemiology
content: Isolated systolic hypertension affects approximately 50% of people older than 70 years old.

title: Isolated systolic hypertension – Clinical significance of treatment
content: The Systolic Hypertension in the Elderly Program (SHEP) in 1991 demonstrated that treating isolated systolic hypertension reduces the risk of strokes and ischaemic heart disease.

title: Isolated systolic hypertension – First-line drug treatment according to SHEP
content: Thiazide diuretics were recommended as first-line agents for treating isolated systolic hypertension according to the SHEP trial.

title: Isolated systolic hypertension – NICE 2011 guideline treatment recommendation
content: The 2011 NICE guidelines recommend treating isolated systolic hypertension using the same stepwise approach as standard hypertension.

title: Stable angina – Definition
content: Stable angina is a clinical condition characterized by chest pain due to myocardial ischemia, typically triggered by exertion or stress and relieved by rest or nitrates.

title: Ivabradine – Mechanism of action
content: Ivabradine reduces heart rate by selectively inhibiting the If ('funny') ion current in the sinoatrial node, thereby decreasing cardiac pacemaker activity.

title: Ivabradine – Therapeutic use in stable angina
content: Ivabradine is used as an anti-anginal drug to reduce heart rate in patients with stable angina.

title: Ivabradine – Adverse effect: Visual disturbances
content: Ivabradine commonly causes visual adverse effects, particularly luminous phenomena such as enhanced brightness or phosphenes.

title: Ivabradine – Adverse effect: Headache
content: Headache is a known adverse effect associated with ivabradine therapy.

title: Ivabradine – Adverse effect: Bradycardia and heart block
content: Ivabradine can cause bradycardia and heart block as adverse cardiac effects due to excessive heart rate reduction.

title: Ivabradine – Comparative efficacy in stable angina
content: There is currently no evidence that ivabradine is superior to existing treatments for stable angina.

title: Loop diuretics – Definition
content: Loop diuretics are medications that inhibit the Na-K-Cl cotransporter (NKCC) in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, reducing NaCl absorption and promoting diuresis.

title: Loop diuretics – Mechanism of action
content: Loop diuretics inhibit the NKCC2 cotransporter located on the apical membrane of the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, decreasing NaCl reabsorption and increasing diuresis.

title: Loop diuretics – NKCC isoforms targeted
content: Loop diuretics specifically target the NKCC2 isoform of the Na-K-Cl cotransporter, which is predominantly expressed in the kidneys.

title: Loop diuretics – Requirement for glomerular filtration
content: Loop diuretics must be filtered by the glomerulus into the renal tubules to reach their site of action on the apical membrane of the thick ascending limb.

title: Loop diuretics – Dose adjustment in renal impairment
content: Patients with poor renal function may require escalating doses of loop diuretics to achieve effective tubular concentrations due to reduced glomerular filtration.

title: Loop diuretics – Indications in heart failure
content: Loop diuretics are indicated for managing both acute heart failure (usually administered intravenously) and chronic heart failure (usually administered orally).

title: Loop diuretics – Indications in resistant hypertension
content: Loop diuretics are used to treat resistant hypertension, particularly in patients with renal impairment.

title: Loop diuretics – Adverse effect: Hypotension
content: Loop diuretics can cause hypotension due to volume depletion and vasodilation.

title: Loop diuretics – Adverse effect: Hyponatraemia
content: Loop diuretics may cause hyponatraemia due to increased sodium excretion.

title: Loop diuretics – Adverse effect: Hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia
content: Loop diuretics can cause hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia by increasing renal excretion of potassium and magnesium.

title: Loop diuretics – Adverse effect: Hypochloraemic alkalosis
content: Loop diuretics may cause hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis due to loss of chloride and volume contraction.

title: Loop diuretics – Adverse effect: Ototoxicity
content: Loop diuretics can cause ototoxicity, potentially leading to hearing loss or tinnitus.

title: Loop diuretics – Adverse effect: Hypocalcaemia
content: Loop diuretics may cause hypocalcaemia by increasing calcium excretion in the urine.

title: Loop diuretics – Adverse effect: Renal impairment
content: Loop diuretics can cause renal impairment due to dehydration and direct nephrotoxic effects.

title: Loop diuretics – Adverse effect: Hyperglycaemia
content: Loop diuretics may cause hyperglycaemia, although this is less common compared to thiazide diuretics.

title: Loop diuretics – Adverse effect: Gout
content: Loop diuretics can precipitate gout by reducing uric acid excretion, leading to hyperuricaemia.

title: Mitral regurgitation – Definition
content: Mitral regurgitation (MR), also known as mitral insufficiency, is a condition where blood leaks back through the mitral valve during systole.

title: Mitral regurgitation – Epidemiology
content: Mitral regurgitation is the second most common valve disease after aortic stenosis.

title: Mitral regurgitation – Anatomy
content: The mitral valve is located between the left atrium and left ventricle of the heart.

title: Mitral regurgitation – Pathophysiology
content: Mitral regurgitation causes blood to flow backward into the left atrium during systole, reducing the efficiency of the heart and decreasing forward blood flow to the body.

title: Mitral regurgitation – Clinical significance of trivial regurgitation
content: Trivial mitral regurgitation is common in otherwise healthy patients and typically does not require treatment.

title: Mitral regurgitation – Progression and myocardial response
content: Severe mitral regurgitation can cause the myocardium to thicken over time due to increased oxygen demand exceeding supply, which may lead to decreased efficiency and irreversible heart failure.

title: Mitral regurgitation – Risk factors
content: Risk factors for mitral regurgitation include female sex, lower body mass, increasing age, renal dysfunction, prior myocardial infarction, prior mitral stenosis or valve prolapse, and collagen disorders such as Marfan's syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

title: Mitral regurgitation – Cause: Coronary artery disease and myocardial infarction
content: Damage to papillary muscles or chordae tendineae from coronary artery disease or myocardial infarction can impair mitral valve function, leading to mitral regurgitation.

title: Mitral regurgitation – Cause: Mitral valve prolapse
content: Mitral valve prolapse occurs when the mitral valve leaflets are deformed and do not close properly, causing backflow and often resulting in a trivial degree of mitral regurgitation.

title: Mitral regurgitation – Cause: Infective endocarditis
content: Infective endocarditis can cause vegetations on the mitral valve, preventing proper closure and leading to mitral regurgitation; patients with abnormal valves are at higher risk.

title: Mitral regurgitation – Cause: Rheumatic fever
content: Rheumatic fever can cause inflammation of the mitral valve leading to mitral regurgitation, although this is uncommon in developed countries.

title: Mitral regurgitation – Cause: Congenital
content: Mitral regurgitation can be caused by congenital abnormalities affecting the mitral valve.

title: Mitral regurgitation – Clinical features: Asymptomatic presentation
content: Most patients with mitral regurgitation are asymptomatic, especially in mild to moderate cases.

title: Myocardial infarction – Risk of complications
content: Patients are at risk of immediate, early, and late complications following a myocardial infarction (MI).

title: Cardiac arrest – Cause after myocardial infarction
content: Cardiac arrest most commonly occurs due to ventricular fibrillation following a myocardial infarction and is the most common cause of death post-MI.

title: Cardiac arrest – Management post-myocardial infarction
content: Patients with cardiac arrest following myocardial infarction are managed according to the Advanced Life Support (ALS) protocol including defibrillation.

title: Cardiogenic shock – Pathophysiology post-myocardial infarction
content: Cardiogenic shock occurs when extensive ventricular myocardium damage reduces ejection fraction, impairing cardiac output after myocardial infarction.

title: Cardiogenic shock – Mechanical causes post-myocardial infarction
content: Mechanical complications such as left ventricular free wall rupture can cause cardiogenic shock after myocardial infarction.

title: Cardiogenic shock – Management
content: Management of cardiogenic shock may require inotropic support and/or intra-aortic balloon pump insertion.

title: Chronic heart failure – Pathophysiology post-myocardial infarction
content: Survivors of the acute phase of myocardial infarction may develop chronic heart failure due to ventricular myocardium dysfunction.

title: Chronic heart failure – Management with loop diuretics
content: Loop diuretics such as furosemide reduce fluid overload in chronic heart failure post-myocardial infarction.

title: Chronic heart failure – Prognosis improvement with ACE-inhibitors and beta-blockers
content: ACE-inhibitors and beta-blockers improve long-term prognosis in patients with chronic heart failure after myocardial infarction.

title: Tachyarrhythmias – Common types post-myocardial infarction
content: Ventricular fibrillation and ventricular tachycardia are common tachyarrhythmias following myocardial infarction.

title: Bradyarrhythmias – Atrioventricular block after inferior myocardial infarction
content: Atrioventricular block is more common following inferior myocardial infarctions.

title: Pericarditis – Incidence and timing post-transmural myocardial infarction
content: Pericarditis occurs in approximately 10% of patients within the first 48 hours following a transmural myocardial infarction.

title: Pericarditis – Clinical features post-myocardial infarction
content: Pericarditis pain is typically worse when lying flat; a pericardial rub may be heard and pericardial effusion can be detected by echocardiogram.

title: Dressler's syndrome – Timing post-myocardial infarction
content: Dressler's syndrome typically occurs 2 to 6 weeks after myocardial infarction.

title: Dressler's syndrome – Pathophysiology
content: Dressler's syndrome is thought to be an autoimmune reaction against antigenic myocardial proteins formed during recovery after myocardial infarction.

title: Dressler's syndrome – Clinical features
content: Dressler's syndrome is characterized by fever, pleuritic chest pain, and pericarditis following myocardial infarction.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Secondary prevention drug therapy
content: All patients following a myocardial infarction should be offered dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus a second antiplatelet agent), an ACE inhibitor, a beta-blocker, and a statin as part of secondary prevention.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Dual antiplatelet therapy options
content: Dual antiplatelet therapy after acute coronary syndrome includes aspirin plus a second antiplatelet agent such as ticagrelor or prasugrel, which have largely replaced clopidogrel as the preferred second agents.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Duration of dual antiplatelet therapy post medically managed ACS
content: For medically managed acute coronary syndrome, ticagrelor is added to aspirin and ticagrelor is stopped after 12 months.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Duration of dual antiplatelet therapy post PCI
content: After percutaneous coronary intervention, prasugrel or ticagrelor is added to aspirin and the second antiplatelet agent is stopped after 12 months.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Adjustment of dual antiplatelet therapy duration
content: The 12-month duration of dual antiplatelet therapy may be altered for patients at high risk of bleeding or those at high risk of further ischaemic events.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Aldosterone antagonist therapy indication post MI
content: Patients who have had an acute myocardial infarction with symptoms and/or signs of heart failure and left ventricular systolic dysfunction should be started on an aldosterone antagonist licensed for post-MI treatment, such as eplerenone.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Timing of aldosterone antagonist initiation post MI
content: Aldosterone antagonist therapy should be initiated within 3 to 14 days after myocardial infarction, preferably after starting ACE inhibitor therapy.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Lifestyle advice: diet
content: Patients post myocardial infarction should be advised to follow a Mediterranean style diet, replacing butter and cheese with plant oil-based products; omega-3 supplements and eating oily fish are not recommended.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Lifestyle advice: exercise
content: Patients post myocardial infarction should be advised to exercise for 20-30 minutes daily until they become slightly breathless.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Sexual activity recommendations post MI
content: Sexual activity may be resumed 4 weeks after an uncomplicated myocardial infarction; patients should be reassured that sexual activity does not increase the likelihood of further myocardial infarction.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – PDE5 inhibitor use post MI
content: Phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors (e.g., sildenafil) may be used 6 months after myocardial infarction but should be avoided in patients prescribed nitrates or nicorandil.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Definition of STEMI
content: ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) is a type of acute coronary syndrome characterized by persistent ST-segment elevation on ECG, indicating transmural myocardial ischemia and infarction.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Aspirin use in STEMI management
content: In the absence of contraindications, all patients with STEMI should be given aspirin as part of initial management to inhibit platelet aggregation and reduce mortality.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – P2Y12-receptor antagonists in STEMI
content: P2Y12-receptor antagonists such as clopidogrel, ticagrelor, and prasugrel are used in STEMI management to inhibit platelet aggregation; ticagrelor is often preferred due to improved outcomes despite a slightly higher bleeding risk.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Prasugrel use in PCI for STEMI
content: Prasugrel, a P2Y12-receptor antagonist, may be considered in STEMI patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) as recommended by SIGN 2016 guidelines.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Anticoagulation in STEMI with PCI
content: Unfractionated heparin is usually administered to STEMI patients undergoing PCI; low-molecular-weight heparin is an alternative anticoagulant option.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Oxygen therapy recommendations in STEMI
content: Routine oxygen administration is not recommended in STEMI; oxygen saturation should be monitored by pulse oximetry, and supplemental oxygen given only if SpO2 is below 94% (88-92% in COPD patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure).

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Primary PCI as gold-standard STEMI treatment
content: Primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is the gold-standard treatment for STEMI but may not be available in all centers.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Thrombolysis indication in STEMI
content: Thrombolysis should be performed in STEMI patients who do not have access to primary PCI.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – tPA mortality benefit over streptokinase in STEMI thrombolysis
content: Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) provides clear mortality benefits compared to streptokinase when used for thrombolysis in STEMI patients.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – Tenecteplase efficacy and administration in STEMI thrombolysis
content: Tenecteplase is easier to administer and has non-inferior efficacy compared to alteplase with a similar adverse effect profile in STEMI thrombolysis.

title: Acute coronary syndromes – ECG assessment 90 minutes after thrombolysis
content: An ECG should be performed 90 minutes after thrombolysis in STEMI patients to assess the degree of ST-segment resolution and reperfusion success.

title: Angina – Definition
content: Angina is chest pain or discomfort caused by myocardial ischaemia due to reduced blood flow to the heart muscle.

title: Nicorandil – Mechanism of action
content: Nicorandil is a potassium-channel activator that causes vasodilation through activation of guanylyl cyclase, resulting in increased cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) levels.

title: Nicorandil – Indications
content: Nicorandil is used as a vasodilatory drug to treat angina.

title: Nicorandil – Adverse effect: Headache
content: Headache is a common adverse effect of nicorandil therapy.

title: Nicorandil – Adverse effect: Flushing
content: Flushing is a common adverse effect of nicorandil therapy.

title: Nicorandil – Adverse effect: Skin, mucosal and eye ulceration
content: Nicorandil can cause ulceration of the skin, mucous membranes, and eyes as an adverse effect.

title: Nicorandil – Adverse effect: Gastrointestinal ulcers including anal ulceration
content: Nicorandil may cause gastrointestinal ulcers, including anal ulceration, as an adverse effect.

title: Nicorandil – Contraindication: Left ventricular failure
content: Nicorandil is contraindicated in patients with left ventricular failure.

title: Hyperlipidaemia – Definition and Treatment with Nicotinic Acid
content: Nicotinic acid (niacin) is used in the treatment of patients with hyperlipidaemia to modify lipid profiles.

title: Nicotinic Acid – Lipid Profile Effects
content: Nicotinic acid lowers cholesterol and triglyceride concentrations and raises HDL cholesterol levels.

title: Nicotinic Acid – Flushing as an Adverse Effect
content: Flushing is a common adverse effect of nicotinic acid and is mediated by prostaglandins.

title: Nicotinic Acid – Impaired Glucose Tolerance as an Adverse Effect
content: Nicotinic acid can cause impaired glucose tolerance as an adverse effect.

title: Nicotinic Acid – Myositis as an Adverse Effect
content: Myositis is a potential adverse effect of nicotinic acid therapy.

title: Nitrates – Definition
content: Nitrates are a group of drugs that have vasodilating effects.

title: Nitrates – Indications
content: Nitrates are mainly indicated for the management of angina and the acute treatment of heart failure.

title: Sublingual glyceryl trinitrate – Use in ischaemic heart disease
content: Sublingual glyceryl trinitrate is the most common drug used in patients with ischaemic heart disease to relieve angina attacks.

title: Nitrates – Mechanism of action
content: Nitrates cause the release of nitric oxide in smooth muscle, which activates guanylate cyclase to convert GTP to cGMP, leading to a fall in intracellular calcium levels.

title: Nitrates – Effects in angina
content: In angina, nitrates dilate coronary arteries and reduce venous return, which decreases left ventricular work and myocardial oxygen demand.

title: Nitrates – Side effects
content: Common side effects of nitrates include hypotension, tachycardia, headaches, and flushing.

title: Nitrate tolerance – Definition
content: Nitrate tolerance is a condition where patients develop reduced efficacy of nitrates after repeated use.

title: Nitrate tolerance – Management with isosorbide mononitrate dosing
content: To reduce nitrate tolerance, the BNF advises taking the second dose of isosorbide mononitrate after 8 hours instead of 12 hours, allowing blood-nitrate levels to fall for 4 hours and maintaining effectiveness.

title: Nitrate tolerance – Effect on modified release isosorbide mononitrate
content: Nitrate tolerance is not seen in patients who take modified release isosorbide mononitrate.

title: Orthostatic hypotension – Definition
content: Orthostatic hypotension is a condition characterized by a drop in blood pressure, usually greater than 20 mm Hg systolic or 10 mm Hg diastolic, within three minutes of standing.

title: Orthostatic hypotension – Epidemiology
content: Orthostatic hypotension is more common in older adults and patients with neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's disease, diabetes, or hypertension.

title: Orthostatic hypotension – Iatrogenic causes
content: Iatrogenic causes of orthostatic hypotension include the use of alpha-blockers, for example those prescribed for benign prostatic hyperplasia.

title: Orthostatic hypotension – Clinical feature: Blood pressure drop
content: A key clinical feature of orthostatic hypotension is a drop in blood pressure greater than 20 mm Hg systolic or 10 mm Hg diastolic within three minutes of standing.

title: Orthostatic hypotension – Presentation: Presyncope
content: Presyncope, a sensation of impending faintness without loss of consciousness, is a common symptom in orthostatic hypotension.

title: Orthostatic hypotension – Presentation: Syncope
content: Syncope, or transient loss of consciousness, can occur as a presentation of orthostatic hypotension.

title: Orthostatic hypotension – Management: Midodrine
content: Midodrine is a treatment option used to manage orthostatic hypotension by increasing vascular tone and blood pressure.

title: Orthostatic hypotension – Management: Fludrocortisone
content: Fludrocortisone is a treatment option for orthostatic hypotension that works by promoting sodium retention and increasing blood volume.

title: Permanent Pacemaker – Definition
content: A permanent pacemaker (PPM) is an electronic device that maintains a consistent and physiologically adequate heart rate when the natural cardiac pacemaker system fails.

title: Cardiac Conduction System – Physiology
content: Electrical impulses originate from the sinoatrial (SA) node in the right atrium, causing atrial contraction, then travel to the atrioventricular (AV) node and along Purkinje fibres, culminating in ventricular contraction and effective cardiac output.

title: Cardiac Conduction System Dysfunction – Pathophysiology
content: Dysfunction at any level of the cardiac conduction system can result in arrhythmias due to impaired electrical impulse generation or conduction.

title: Permanent Pacemaker – Mechanism of Action
content: A permanent pacemaker delivers timed electrical stimuli to the myocardium to promote effective contractions and maintain circulation when intrinsic conduction is abnormal.

title: Permanent Pacemaker – Indications
content: Indications for permanent pacemaker insertion include persistent symptomatic bradycardia such as sick sinus syndrome, complete heart block, Mobitz type II AV block, and persistent AV block after myocardial infarction.

title: Permanent Pacemaker – Nomenclature Code First Position
content: The first position in the pacemaker code denotes the chamber paced: V for ventricle, A for atrium, D for dual (both atrium and ventricle), and O for none (no pacing).

title: Permanent Pacemaker – Nomenclature Code Second Position
content: The second position in the pacemaker code denotes the chamber sensed: V for ventricle, A for atrium, D for dual (both atrium and ventricle), and O for none (no sensing).

title: Permanent Pacemaker – Nomenclature Code Third Position
content: The third position in the pacemaker code denotes the response to sensing: I for inhibited pacing, T for triggered pacing, D for dual (both inhibited and triggered), and O for none (no response to sensing).

title: Temporary pacemaker – Indication: symptomatic bradycardia unresponsive to atropine
content: A temporary pacemaker is indicated in patients with symptomatic or haemodynamically unstable bradycardia that does not respond to atropine administration.

title: Temporary pacemaker – Indication: type 2 or complete heart block post-anterior myocardial infarction
content: Temporary pacing is indicated for patients who develop type 2 or complete heart block following an anterior myocardial infarction.

title: Complete heart block post-inferior myocardial infarction – Conservative management if asymptomatic and haemodynamically stable
content: Complete heart block occurring after an inferior myocardial infarction is common and can be managed conservatively if the patient is asymptomatic and haemodynamically stable, without the need for temporary pacing.

title: Temporary pacemaker – Indication: trifascicular block prior to surgery
content: A temporary pacemaker is indicated in patients with trifascicular block who are undergoing surgery to prevent perioperative conduction disturbances.

title: Parenteral anticoagulation – Indications
content: Parenteral anticoagulants are used for the prevention of venous thromboembolism and in the management of acute coronary syndrome.

title: Fondaparinux – Mechanism of action
content: Fondaparinux activates antithrombin III, which potentiates the inhibition of coagulation factor Xa.

title: Fondaparinux – Route of administration
content: Fondaparinux is administered via subcutaneous injection.

title: Direct thrombin inhibitors – Examples
content: Examples of direct thrombin inhibitors include bivalirudin and dabigatran.

title: Direct thrombin inhibitors – Route of administration
content: Direct thrombin inhibitors such as bivalirudin are generally administered intravenously.

title: Dabigatran – Classification and route
content: Dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor taken orally and is often grouped with direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs).

title: Bradycardia – Definition
content: Bradycardia is a peri-arrest rhythm characterized by a slower than normal heart rate that may lead to haemodynamic compromise.

title: Bradycardia – Haemodynamic compromise indicators
content: Haemodynamic compromise in bradycardia is indicated by adverse signs such as shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia, and heart failure.

title: Shock – Presentation in bradycardia
content: Shock as an adverse sign in bradycardia includes hypotension (systolic blood pressure < 90 mmHg), pallor, sweating, cold clammy extremities, confusion, or impaired consciousness.

title: Bradycardia – First line treatment for haemodynamic compromise
content: Atropine 500 mcg IV is the first line treatment for bradycardia with haemodynamic compromise.

title: Bradycardia – Second line treatments for unsatisfactory atropine response
content: If atropine response is unsatisfactory, treatments include atropine up to 3 mg total, transcutaneous pacing, and isoprenaline or adrenaline infusion titrated to response.

title: Bradycardia – Specialist intervention for refractory cases
content: Specialist help should be sought for consideration of transvenous pacing if there is no response to atropine, transcutaneous pacing, or inotropic infusions.

title: Bradycardia – Risk factors for asystole
content: Risk factors for asystole in bradycardia include complete heart block with broad complex QRS, recent asystole, Mobitz type II AV block, and ventricular pause longer than 3 seconds.

title: Bradycardia – Specialist referral despite satisfactory atropine response if risk factors present
content: Even with a satisfactory atropine response, specialist help is indicated to consider transvenous pacing if risk factors for asystole are present.

title: Peri-arrest tachycardia – unified treatment algorithm
content: The 2015 Resuscitation Council (UK) guidelines replaced separate algorithms for broad-complex tachycardia, narrow-complex tachycardia, and atrial fibrillation with one unified treatment algorithm for peri-arrest tachycardias.

title: Peri-arrest tachycardia – initial patient assessment
content: Initial management of peri-arrest tachycardia includes a basic ABC (Airway, Breathing, Circulation) assessment followed by classification of patients as stable or unstable based on the presence of adverse signs.

title: Peri-arrest tachycardia – adverse signs indicating instability
content: Adverse signs indicating instability in peri-arrest tachycardia include shock (hypotension with systolic blood pressure < 90 mmHg, pallor, sweating, cold clammy extremities, confusion or impaired consciousness), syncope, myocardial ischaemia, and heart failure.

title: Peri-arrest tachycardia – management of unstable patients
content: Unstable patients with peri-arrest tachycardia should receive synchronised DC shocks; up to three shocks can be administered before seeking expert help.

title: Peri-arrest tachycardia – QRS complex classification for treatment
content: Treatment after initial stabilisation is guided by QRS complex width (narrow or broad) and rhythm regularity (regular or irregular).

title: Broad-complex tachycardia – regular rhythm assumption
content: Regular broad-complex tachycardia is assumed to be ventricular tachycardia unless previously confirmed as supraventricular tachycardia with bundle branch block.

title: Broad-complex tachycardia – regular rhythm management
content: Management of regular broad-complex tachycardia includes a loading dose of amiodarone followed by a 24-hour infusion.

title: Broad-complex tachycardia – irregular rhythm management
content: Irregular broad-complex tachycardia requires expert help; possible causes include atrial fibrillation with bundle branch block, atrial fibrillation with ventricular pre-excitation, and torsade de pointes.

title: Narrow-complex tachycardia – regular rhythm initial management
content: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia is initially managed with vagal manoeuvres followed by intravenous adenosine.

title: Narrow-complex tachycardia – regular rhythm secondary management
content: If vagal manoeuvres and IV adenosine are unsuccessful in regular narrow-complex tachycardia, consider atrial flutter and control the rate using beta-blockers.

title: Narrow-complex tachycardia – irregular rhythm probable diagnosis
content: Irregular narrow-complex tachycardia is probably atrial fibrillation.

title: Atrial fibrillation – cardioversion indication in peri-arrest tachycardia
content: In atrial fibrillation with onset less than 48 hours, consider electrical or chemical cardioversion.

title: Atrial fibrillation – rate control in peri-arrest tachycardia
content: Rate control in atrial fibrillation is usually achieved with beta-blockers unless contraindicated.

title: Postural hypotension – Definition
content: Postural hypotension is defined as a fall of systolic blood pressure greater than 20 mmHg on standing.

title: Postural hypotension – Cause: Hypovolaemia
content: Hypovolaemia is a cause of postural hypotension.

title: Postural hypotension – Cause: Autonomic dysfunction
content: Autonomic dysfunction is a cause of postural hypotension.

title: Postural hypotension – Cause: Autonomic dysfunction in diabetes
content: Diabetes can cause autonomic dysfunction leading to postural hypotension.

title: Postural hypotension – Cause: Autonomic dysfunction in Parkinson's disease
content: Parkinson's disease can cause autonomic dysfunction leading to postural hypotension.

title: Postural hypotension – Cause: Drugs
content: Certain drugs can cause postural hypotension.

title: Postural hypotension – Cause: Drugs – Diuretics
content: Diuretics are drugs that can cause postural hypotension.

title: Postural hypotension – Cause: Drugs – Antihypertensives
content: Antihypertensive drugs can cause postural hypotension.

title: Postural hypotension – Cause: Drugs – L-dopa
content: L-dopa is a drug that can cause postural hypotension.

title: Postural hypotension – Cause: Drugs – Phenothiazines
content: Phenothiazines are drugs that can cause postural hypotension.

title: Postural hypotension – Cause: Drugs – Antidepressants
content: Antidepressants are drugs that can cause postural hypotension.

title: Postural hypotension – Cause: Drugs – Sedatives
content: Sedatives are drugs that can cause postural hypotension.

title: Postural hypotension – Cause: Alcohol
content: Alcohol consumption can cause postural hypotension.

title: Potassium-sparing diuretics – Classification
content: Potassium-sparing diuretics are divided into epithelial sodium channel blockers (amiloride and triamterene) and aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone and eplerenone).

title: Potassium-sparing diuretics – Hyperkalaemia risk with ACE inhibitors
content: Potassium-sparing diuretics should be used with caution in patients taking ACE inhibitors because they can precipitate hyperkalaemia.

title: Amiloride – Mechanism of action
content: Amiloride blocks the epithelial sodium channel in the distal convoluted tubule of the kidney.

title: Amiloride – Clinical use
content: Amiloride is a weak diuretic usually given with thiazide or loop diuretics as an alternative to potassium supplementation to prevent hypokalaemia.

title: Aldosterone antagonists – Site of action
content: Aldosterone antagonists such as spironolactone act in the cortical collecting duct of the kidney.

title: Aldosterone antagonists – Indications in ascites
content: Spironolactone is used in ascites due to cirrhosis where secondary hyperaldosteronism occurs; relatively large doses such as 100-200 mg are often used.

title: Aldosterone antagonists – Indications in heart failure
content: Spironolactone is indicated in the management of heart failure.

title: Aldosterone antagonists – Indications in nephrotic syndrome
content: Spironolactone is used in the management of nephrotic syndrome.

title: Aldosterone antagonists – Indications in Conn's syndrome
content: Spironolactone is indicated in Conn's syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism).

title: Premature ventricular complexes – Definition
content: Premature ventricular complexes (PVCs) are beats originating in the ventricular myocardium and are also known as premature ventricular beats or ventricular extrasystoles.

title: Premature ventricular complexes – Epidemiology
content: Premature ventricular complexes are common and occur in a wide population group, including individuals with and without underlying cardiac disease.

title: Premature ventricular complexes – Aetiology idiopathic
content: The vast majority of premature ventricular complexes are idiopathic, occurring without identifiable underlying cardiac disease.

title: Premature ventricular complexes – Aetiology hypertension
content: Hypertension is a recognized cause of premature ventricular complexes.

title: Premature ventricular complexes – Aetiology myocardial infarction
content: Myocardial infarction is a recognized cause of premature ventricular complexes.

title: Premature ventricular complexes – Clinical features asymptomatic
content: The vast majority of patients with premature ventricular complexes are asymptomatic.

title: Premature ventricular complexes – Clinical features palpitations
content: Some patients with premature ventricular complexes experience palpitations, typically described as the sensation of a 'skipped beat'.

title: Premature ventricular complexes – Clinical features pulse irregularity
content: During regular premature ventricular complexes, the pulse will feel irregular.

title: Premature ventricular complexes – ECG features
content: Premature ventricular complexes originate in the ventricles and produce a wide QRS complex on ECG.

title: Premature ventricular complexes – Management asymptomatic without cardiac disease
content: Asymptomatic patients with premature ventricular complexes and no evidence of underlying cardiac disease do not require any further management.

title: Aortic valve disease – Common valves requiring replacement
content: The aortic valve is one of the most common valves that require replacement.

title: Mitral valve disease – Common valves requiring replacement
content: The mitral valve is one of the most common valves that require replacement.

title: Prosthetic heart valves – Types of replacement valves
content: There are two main types of prosthetic heart valves used for replacement: biological (bioprosthetic) and mechanical valves.

title: Bioprosthetic valves – Origin
content: Biological (bioprosthetic) valves are usually derived from bovine or porcine tissue.

title: Bioprosthetic valves – Major disadvantage
content: Bioprosthetic valves have a major disadvantage of structural deterioration and calcification over time.

title: Bioprosthetic valves – Age considerations for implantation
content: Most older patients receive bioprosthetic valves: those over 65 years for aortic valve replacement and over 70 years for mitral valve replacement.

title: Bioprosthetic valves – Anticoagulation requirements
content: Long-term anticoagulation is usually not needed with bioprosthetic valves; warfarin may be given for the first 3 months depending on patient factors, and low-dose aspirin is given long-term.

title: Mechanical valves – Common types implanted
content: The most common mechanical valve now implanted is the bileaflet valve; ball-and-cage valves are rarely used nowadays.

title: Mechanical valves – Failure rate
content: Mechanical valves have a low failure rate.

title: Mechanical valves – Major disadvantage
content: Mechanical valves have an increased risk of thrombosis, necessitating long-term anticoagulation.

title: Mechanical valves – Preferred anticoagulant
content: Warfarin is preferred over direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) for patients with mechanical heart valves.

title: Mechanical valves – Aspirin use according to 2017 ESC guidelines
content: Following the 2017 European Society of Cardiology guidelines, aspirin is only given in addition to warfarin if there is an additional indication such as ischaemic heart disease.

title: Mechanical valves – Target INR values
content: The target international normalized ratio (INR) for patients with mechanical valves is 3.0 for aortic valve replacements and 3.5 for mitral valve replacements.

title: Prosthetic heart valves – Endocarditis prophylaxis guidelines
content: According to the 2008 NICE guidelines, antibiotic prophylaxis for endocarditis is no longer recommended for common procedures such as dental work in patients with prosthetic heart valves.

title: Pulmonary artery occlusion pressure monitoring – Definition
content: Pulmonary artery occlusion pressure (PAOP) is an indirect measure of left atrial pressure and thus reflects the filling pressure of the left heart.

title: Pulmonary artery occlusion pressure monitoring – Pathophysiology
content: Low resistance in the pulmonary venous system allows PAOP to be measured indirectly by occluding a pulmonary artery branch with a balloon-tipped catheter.

title: Pulmonary artery occlusion pressure monitoring – Measurement technique
content: The most accurate PAOP measurement is obtained by inflating the balloon at the catheter tip and floating it to occlude a pulmonary artery branch; if occlusion is not possible, the measurement reflects pulmonary artery end diastolic pressure.

title: Pulmonary artery occlusion pressure – Normal values
content: Normal pulmonary artery occlusion pressure ranges from 8 to 12 mmHg.

title: Pulmonary artery occlusion pressure – Low values and causes
content: A PAOP less than 5 mmHg indicates hypovolaemia; if low PAOP is accompanied by pulmonary oedema, it suggests acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).

title: Pulmonary artery occlusion pressure – High values and cause
content: A PAOP greater than 18 mmHg indicates fluid overload.

title: Systemic vascular resistance – Definition and calculation
content: Systemic vascular resistance (SVR) is derived from mean aortic pressure, mean right atrial pressure, and cardiac output, calculated as SVR = 80 × (mean aortic pressure − mean right atrial pressure) / cardiac output.

title: Pulmonary artery occlusion pressure monitoring – Clinical utility
content: Combining PAOP measurements with systemic vascular resistance and cardiac output allows accurate classification of patients' hemodynamic status.

title: Pulmonary embolism – Definition
content: Pulmonary embolism is a condition where one or more emboli obstruct the pulmonary arteries, leading to impaired blood flow in the lungs.

title: Pulmonary embolism – Chest pain characteristic
content: Chest pain in pulmonary embolism is typically pleuritic, meaning it worsens with breathing or coughing.

title: Pulmonary embolism – Dyspnoea
content: Dyspnoea, or shortness of breath, is a common presenting symptom of pulmonary embolism.

title: Pulmonary embolism – Haemoptysis
content: Haemoptysis, or coughing up blood, can be a presenting symptom in pulmonary embolism.

title: Pulmonary embolism – Tachycardia
content: Tachycardia, defined as a heart rate greater than 100 beats per minute, is a common sign in pulmonary embolism.

title: Pulmonary embolism – Tachypnoea
content: Tachypnoea, defined as a respiratory rate greater than 16 breaths per minute, is present in most patients with pulmonary embolism.

title: Pulmonary embolism – Respiratory examination findings
content: The chest examination in pulmonary embolism is classically clear, but real-world clinical practice often reveals abnormal findings such as crackles.

title: Pulmonary embolism – Frequency of classic triad presentation
content: Only about 10% of patients with pulmonary embolism present with the classic triad of pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea, and haemoptysis.

title: Pulmonary embolism – Diagnostic challenge
content: Pulmonary embolism can present with virtually any cardiorespiratory symptom or sign depending on the embolus location and size, making diagnosis difficult.

title: Pulmonary embolism – Tachypnoea frequency (PIOPED study)
content: The PIOPED study found tachypnoea (respiratory rate >16/min) in 96% of patients diagnosed with pulmonary embolism.

title: Pulmonary embolism – Crackles frequency (PIOPED study)
content: Crackles were present in 58% of patients with pulmonary embolism according to the PIOPED study.

title: Pulmonary embolism – Tachycardia frequency (PIOPED study)
content: Tachycardia (heart rate >100/min) was observed in 44% of pulmonary embolism patients in the PIOPED study.

title: Pulmonary embolism – Fever frequency (PIOPED study)
content: Fever, defined as temperature >37.8°C, was present in 43% of patients with pulmonary embolism in the PIOPED study.

title: Pulmonary embolism – Well's criteria use tachycardia
content: The Well's criteria for diagnosing pulmonary embolism include tachycardia but do not include tachypnoea as a criterion.

title: Pulmonary embolism – Clinical presentation frequency
content: Approximately 10% of patients with pulmonary embolism present with the classic triad of pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea, and haemoptysis.

title: Pulmonary embolism – Variability of clinical presentation
content: Pulmonary embolism can present with virtually any cardiorespiratory symptom or sign depending on the embolus location and size, making diagnosis challenging.

title: Pulmonary embolism – Tachypnea frequency
content: Tachypnea, defined as respiratory rate greater than 20 breaths per minute, occurs in 96% of patients diagnosed with pulmonary embolism according to the PIOPED study.

title: Pulmonary embolism – Crackles frequency
content: Crackles are present in 58% of patients with pulmonary embolism as reported by the PIOPED study.

title: Pulmonary embolism – Tachycardia frequency
content: Tachycardia, defined as heart rate greater than 100 beats per minute, occurs in 44% of pulmonary embolism patients according to the PIOPED study.

title: Pulmonary embolism – Fever frequency
content: Fever, defined as temperature above 37.8°C, is observed in 43% of patients with pulmonary embolism as per the PIOPED study.

title: Pulmonary embolism – Wells criteria use tachycardia
content: The Wells criteria for diagnosing pulmonary embolism include tachycardia but do not include tachypnea as a diagnostic parameter.

title: Pulmonary embolism – Initial assessment components
content: All patients with symptoms or signs suggestive of pulmonary embolism should undergo a detailed history, physical examination, and chest X-ray to exclude alternative diagnoses.

title: Pulmonary embolism – Pulmonary embolism rule-out criteria (PERC) purpose
content: The PERC rule is used to rule out pulmonary embolism in patients with low pre-test probability, providing reassurance that PE is unlikely if all criteria are absent.

title: Pulmonary embolism – PERC rule application criteria
content: The PERC rule should be applied when clinical suspicion of pulmonary embolism is low (pre-test probability <15%) and other diagnoses are feasible.

title: Pulmonary embolism – NICE 2020 guideline update on PERC
content: NICE 2020 guidelines recommend the use of the PERC rule to safely exclude pulmonary embolism in low-risk patients based on clinical impression and initial investigations.

title: Pulmonary embolism – First-line anticoagulant treatment
content: Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are recommended as first-line treatment for most people with venous thromboembolism (VTE), including pulmonary embolism (PE), according to NICE 2020 guidelines.

title: Pulmonary embolism – Anticoagulant choice in active cancer
content: DOACs are now recommended over low-molecular weight heparin (LMWH) for anticoagulation in patients with active cancer and venous thromboembolism, replacing previous guidelines.

title: Pulmonary embolism – Outpatient treatment in low-risk patients
content: Outpatient management is recommended for patients with low-risk pulmonary embolism, supported by NICE 2020 guidelines, reflecting a shift from routine hospital admission.

title: Pulmonary embolism – Risk stratification for outpatient treatment
content: NICE recommends using a validated risk stratification tool to determine suitability for outpatient treatment in pulmonary embolism, though no specific tool is mandated.

title: Pulmonary embolism – Use of Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index (PESI) score
content: The 2018 British Society guidelines support using the Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index (PESI) score as a risk stratification tool to identify low-risk PE patients suitable for outpatient management.

title: Pulmonary embolism – Criteria for outpatient treatment eligibility
content: Key criteria for outpatient treatment of pulmonary embolism include haemodynamic stability, absence of significant comorbidities, and adequate home support.

title: Pulmonary embolism – Anticoagulant therapy as cornerstone of management
content: Anticoagulant therapy is the cornerstone of venous thromboembolism management, historically using warfarin with heparin bridging, now increasingly replaced by DOACs.

title: Pulmonary embolism – Use of DOACs at diagnosis suspicion
content: NICE 2020 guidelines recommend starting direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) once pulmonary embolism is suspected, continuing if diagnosis is confirmed, replacing previous LMWH bridging.

title: Pulmonary embolism – First-line DOAC options
content: Apixaban and rivaroxaban, both direct oral anticoagulants, should be offered as first-line anticoagulant treatment following pulmonary embolism diagnosis.

title: Pulmonary embolism – Routine cancer screening after VTE diagnosis
content: Routine cancer screening is no longer recommended following a diagnosis of venous thromboembolism, according to NICE 2020 guidelines.

title: Pulsus paradoxus – Definition
content: Pulsus paradoxus is defined as a greater than normal (more than 10 mmHg) fall in systolic blood pressure during inspiration, resulting in a faint or absent pulse during inspiration.

title: Pulsus paradoxus – Associated conditions
content: Pulsus paradoxus is commonly observed in severe asthma and cardiac tamponade.

title: Slow-rising pulse – Definition
content: A slow-rising or plateau pulse is characterized by a delayed and prolonged upstroke of the arterial pulse wave.

title: Slow-rising pulse – Associated condition
content: A slow-rising pulse is typically associated with aortic stenosis.

title: Collapsing pulse – Definition
content: A collapsing pulse is characterized by a rapid upstroke and downstroke with a sudden collapse of the arterial pulse.

title: Collapsing pulse – Associated conditions
content: Collapsing pulse is associated with aortic regurgitation, patent ductus arteriosus, and hyperkinetic states such as anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, fever, exercise, and pregnancy.

title: Pulsus alternans – Definition
content: Pulsus alternans is the regular alternation of the force of the arterial pulse with each heartbeat.

title: Pulsus alternans – Associated condition
content: Pulsus alternans is a sign of severe left ventricular failure (LVF).

title: Bisferiens pulse – Definition
content: Bisferiens pulse is characterized by a 'double pulse' with two systolic peaks in the arterial waveform.

title: Bisferiens pulse – Associated condition
content: Bisferiens pulse is typically seen in mixed aortic valve disease.

title: Jerky pulse – Definition
content: A 'jerky' pulse is characterized by a forceful and brisk arterial pulse with a rapid upstroke and a sudden collapse.

title: Jerky pulse – Associated condition
content: A jerky pulse is associated with hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM).

title: Bisferiens pulse – Occasional association with HOCM
content: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) may occasionally be associated with a bisferiens pulse.

title: Rheumatic fever – Definition
content: Rheumatic fever is an immunological reaction that develops 2-4 weeks after a Streptococcus pyogenes infection.

title: Rheumatic fever – Pathophysiology: Immune activation
content: Streptococcus pyogenes infection activates the innate immune system leading to antigen presentation to T cells.

title: Rheumatic fever – Pathophysiology: Adaptive immune response
content: B and T cells produce IgG and IgM antibodies and activate CD4+ T cells in response to Streptococcus pyogenes antigens.

title: Rheumatic fever – Pathophysiology: Molecular mimicry and cross-reactivity
content: Antibodies against Streptococcus pyogenes M protein cross-react with cardiac myosin and arterial smooth muscle, causing a type II hypersensitivity reaction.

title: Rheumatic fever – Pathophysiology: Aschoff bodies
content: Aschoff bodies are granulomatous nodules found in the myocardium of patients with rheumatic fever.

title: Rheumatic fever – Diagnostic criteria: Evidence of recent streptococcal infection
content: Diagnosis requires evidence of recent streptococcal infection demonstrated by raised or rising streptococcal antibodies, positive throat swab, or positive rapid group A streptococcal antigen test.

title: Rheumatic fever – Diagnostic criteria: Major criteria overview
content: Diagnosis requires either two major criteria or one major plus two minor criteria in the presence of recent streptococcal infection.

title: Rheumatic fever – Major criteria: Erythema marginatum
content: Erythema marginatum is a major diagnostic criterion characterized by a distinctive rash seen in rheumatic fever.

title: Rheumatic fever – Major criteria: Sydenham's chorea
content: Sydenham's chorea is a late neurological manifestation of rheumatic fever characterized by involuntary, rapid movements.

title: Rheumatic fever – Major criteria: Polyarthritis
content: Polyarthritis involving large joints is a major diagnostic criterion of rheumatic fever.

title: Rheumatic fever – Major criteria: Carditis and valvulitis
content: Carditis and valvulitis, including pancarditis, are major criteria; diagnosis requires evidence of endocarditis manifesting as valvulitis with a regurgitant murmur.

title: Rheumatic fever – Major criteria: Subcutaneous nodules
content: Subcutaneous nodules are painless lumps over bony prominences and are a major diagnostic criterion in rheumatic fever.

title: Rheumatic fever – Minor criteria: Raised ESR or CRP
content: Elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) or C-reactive protein (CRP) levels are minor diagnostic criteria in rheumatic fever.

title: Rheumatic fever – Minor criteria: Pyrexia
content: Fever (pyrexia) is a minor diagnostic criterion in rheumatic fever.

title: Rheumatic fever – Minor criteria: Arthralgia
content: Arthralgia, or joint pain without arthritis, is a minor diagnostic criterion in rheumatic fever.

title: Rheumatic fever – Minor criteria: Prolonged PR interval
content: A prolonged PR interval on electrocardiogram is a minor diagnostic criterion in rheumatic fever.

title: Rheumatic fever – Management: Antibiotic therapy
content: Oral penicillin V is the first-line antibiotic treatment to eradicate Streptococcus pyogenes in rheumatic fever.

title: Rheumatic fever – Management: Anti-inflammatory treatment
content: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are first-line agents for controlling inflammation in rheumatic fever.

title: Rheumatic fever – Management: Treatment of complications
content: Management includes treatment of complications such as heart failure that may develop secondary to rheumatic fever.

title: Saphenous vein – Definition
content: The saphenous veins are superficial veins of the lower limb consisting of the long (great) saphenous vein and the short (small) saphenous vein.

title: Long saphenous vein – Clinical use in bypass surgery
content: The long saphenous vein may be harvested for use as a conduit in bypass surgery.

title: Long saphenous vein – Treatment of varicose veins
content: The long saphenous vein can be removed as treatment for varicose veins associated with saphenofemoral junction incompetence.

title: Long saphenous vein – Origin
content: The long saphenous vein originates at the first digit of the foot where the dorsal vein merges with the dorsal venous arch.

title: Long saphenous vein – Course at the medial malleolus and leg
content: The long saphenous vein passes anterior to the medial malleolus and runs up the medial side of the leg.

title: Long saphenous vein – Course at the knee
content: At the knee, the long saphenous vein runs over the posterior border of the medial epicondyle of the femur bone.

title: Long saphenous vein – Course on the thigh and saphenous opening
content: The long saphenous vein passes laterally to lie on the anterior surface of the thigh before entering the saphenous opening in the fascia lata.

title: Long saphenous vein – Termination at saphenofemoral junction
content: The long saphenous vein joins the femoral vein in the femoral triangle region at the saphenofemoral junction.

title: Long saphenous vein – Tributaries
content: The tributaries of the long saphenous vein include the medial marginal vein, superficial epigastric vein, superficial iliac circumflex vein, and superficial external pudendal veins.

title: Short saphenous vein – Origin
content: The short saphenous vein originates at the fifth digit of the foot where the dorsal vein merges with the dorsal venous arch, which connects to the great saphenous vein.

title: Short saphenous vein – Course around the foot and leg
content: The short saphenous vein passes around the lateral aspect of the foot, inferior and posterior to the lateral malleolus, and runs along the posterior aspect of the leg alongside the sural nerve.

title: Short saphenous vein – Course at the knee and drainage
content: The short saphenous vein passes between the heads of the gastrocnemius muscle and drains into the popliteal vein approximately at or above the level of the knee joint.

title: Atrial Fibrillation – Anticoagulation Risk Assessment
content: The CHA2DS2-VASc score is used to determine the need for anticoagulation therapy in patients with atrial fibrillation to prevent stroke.

title: Heart Failure – Severity Classification
content: The NYHA (New York Heart Association) classification is a heart failure severity scale that categorizes patients based on symptoms and physical activity limitations.

title: Deep Vein Thrombosis – Risk Estimation
content: The Wells score helps estimate the probability of a patient having deep vein thrombosis based on clinical features and risk factors.

title: Pneumonia – Prognosis Assessment
content: The CURB-65 score is used to assess the prognosis of patients with pneumonia and guide management decisions.

title: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea – Symptom Assessment
content: The Epworth Sleepiness Scale is used to assess daytime sleepiness in patients suspected of having obstructive sleep apnoea.

title: Prostate Cancer – Prognosis Indicator
content: The Gleason score indicates the prognosis of prostate cancer based on histological grading of tumor tissue.

title: Newborn – Immediate Health Assessment
content: The APGAR score assesses the health of a newborn immediately after birth by evaluating Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, and Respiration.

title: Labour – Induction Readiness Assessment
content: The Bishop score is used to assess the likelihood that induction of labour will be required based on cervical status and fetal position.

title: Pressure Ulcer – Risk Assessment
content: The Waterlow score assesses the risk of a patient developing pressure sores based on multiple risk factors including mobility and skin condition.

title: Osteoporosis – Fracture Risk Assessment
content: The FRAX tool, developed by WHO, calculates a patient's 10-year risk of developing an osteoporosis-related fracture.

title: Statins – Mechanism of action
content: Statins inhibit the action of HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in hepatic cholesterol synthesis.

title: Statins – Myopathy adverse effects
content: Statin-induced myopathy includes myalgia, myositis, rhabdomyolysis, and asymptomatic raised creatine kinase.

title: Statins – Risk factors for myopathy
content: Risk factors for statin-induced myopathy include advanced age, female sex, low body mass index, and multisystem diseases such as diabetes mellitus.

title: Statins – Myopathy risk by statin lipophilicity
content: Myopathy is more common with lipophilic statins (simvastatin, atorvastatin) than with relatively hydrophilic statins (rosuvastatin, pravastatin, fluvastatin).

title: Statins – Liver impairment monitoring
content: NICE 2014 guidelines recommend checking liver function tests at baseline, 3 months, and 12 months during statin therapy; treatment should be discontinued if serum transaminases rise to and persist at three times the upper limit of normal.

title: Statins – Intracerebral haemorrhage risk in secondary stroke prevention
content: Statins may increase the risk of intracerebral haemorrhage in patients with a history of stroke; this risk is not observed in primary prevention.

title: Statins – Recommendation to avoid in patients with prior intracerebral haemorrhage
content: The Royal College of Physicians recommends avoiding statins in patients with a history of intracerebral haemorrhage.

title: Statins – Drug interactions with macrolides
content: Macrolide antibiotics such as erythromycin and clarithromycin interact with statins; statin therapy should be stopped until completion of the macrolide course.

title: Statins – Contraindication in pregnancy
content: Statins are contraindicated during pregnancy.

title: Statins – Indications in established cardiovascular disease
content: All patients with established cardiovascular disease including stroke, transient ischemic attack, ischemic heart disease, and peripheral arterial disease should receive statins.

title: Statins – Indications based on 10-year cardiovascular risk
content: NICE 2014 recommends statin therapy for anyone with a 10-year cardiovascular risk of 10% or greater.

title: Statins – Use in type 2 diabetes mellitus
content: Patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus should be assessed using QRISK2 to determine the need for statin therapy.

title: Statins – Use in type 1 diabetes mellitus
content: Patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus diagnosed more than 10 years ago, or aged over 40 years, or with established nephropathy should receive statins.

title: Statins – Timing of administration
content: Statins should be taken at night because the majority of cholesterol synthesis occurs during this time; this is especially important for simvastatin due to its shorter half-life.

title: Subclavian artery – Definition and function
content: The subclavian arteries are major vessels of the upper thorax that supply blood to the upper limbs, neck, brain, and thoracic wall.

title: Subclavian artery – Origin of left subclavian artery
content: The left subclavian artery arises directly from the arch of the aorta.

title: Subclavian artery – Origin of right subclavian artery
content: The right subclavian artery originates from the brachiocephalic trunk, which bifurcates into the right subclavian and right common carotid arteries.

title: Subclavian artery – Course and anatomical relations
content: The subclavian artery travels laterally, arching upward and laterally behind the clavicle, passing between the anterior and middle scalene muscles within the scalene triangle; it lies posterior to scalenus anterior and anterior to scalenus medius.

title: Subclavian artery – Transition to axillary artery
content: As the subclavian artery crosses the lateral border of the first rib, it becomes the axillary artery, which continues to supply the upper limb.

title: Subclavian artery – Accessibility in subclavian triangle
content: In the subclavian triangle, the subclavian artery is relatively superficial and accessible for clinical procedures.

title: Subclavian artery – Vertebral artery branch anatomy and function
content: The vertebral artery ascends through the transverse foramina of C6 to C1 vertebrae to enter the foramen magnum and contributes to the circle of Willis.

title: Subclavian artery – Internal thoracic artery branch anatomy and function
content: The internal thoracic artery (internal mammary artery) descends into the thorax to supply the anterior chest wall and breasts.

title: Subclavian artery – Thyrocervical trunk branch anatomy and function
content: The thyrocervical trunk gives off branches to the thyroid gland, neck muscles, and scapular region.

title: Subclavian artery – Costocervical trunk branch anatomy and function
content: The costocervical trunk divides into deep cervical and superior intercostal arteries, supplying the upper intercostal spaces and deep neck muscles.

title: Subclavian artery – Dorsal scapular artery anatomy and function
content: The dorsal scapular artery supplies the levator scapulae and rhomboid muscles and sometimes arises from the transverse cervical artery.

title: Subclavian steal syndrome – Pathophysiology
content: Subclavian steal syndrome occurs due to proximal subclavian artery stenosis or occlusion causing reversal of blood flow in the vertebral artery, leading to vertebrobasilar insufficiency.

title: Subclavian steal syndrome – Clinical features
content: Symptoms of subclavian steal syndrome include dizziness, syncope, and arm claudication due to vertebrobasilar insufficiency.

title: Thoracic outlet syndrome – Pathophysiology
content: Thoracic outlet syndrome involves compression of the subclavian artery, vein, and/or brachial plexus as they pass through the scalene triangle.

title: Thoracic outlet syndrome – Clinical features
content: Thoracic outlet syndrome presents with upper limb ischaemia, numbness, and weakness due to vascular and/or neural compression.

title: Supraventricular tachycardia – Definition
content: Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) refers to any tachycardia that is not ventricular in origin, commonly used to describe paroxysmal SVT.

title: Supraventricular tachycardia – Pathophysiology: AVNRT
content: Atrioventricular nodal re-entry tachycardia (AVNRT) is the typical mechanism causing sudden onset narrow complex tachycardia in SVT.

title: Supraventricular tachycardia – Pathophysiology: AVRT and junctional tachycardias
content: Other causes of SVT include atrioventricular re-entry tachycardias (AVRT) and junctional tachycardias.

title: Supraventricular tachycardia – Clinical feature: sudden onset narrow complex tachycardia
content: Episodes of SVT are characterised by sudden onset of narrow complex tachycardia.

title: Supraventricular tachycardia – Acute management: vagal manoeuvres
content: Vagal manoeuvres such as the Valsalva manoeuvre and carotid sinus massage are first-line acute treatments for SVT.

title: Supraventricular tachycardia – Acute management: Valsalva manoeuvre technique
content: The Valsalva manoeuvre involves trying to blow into an empty plastic syringe to increase vagal tone and terminate SVT.

title: Supraventricular tachycardia – Acute management: intravenous adenosine dosing
content: Intravenous adenosine is given as a rapid IV bolus starting with 6 mg, followed by 12 mg if unsuccessful, and then 18 mg if further doses are needed.

title: Supraventricular tachycardia – Acute management: adenosine contraindications
content: Adenosine is contraindicated in asthmatic patients; verapamil is preferred in these cases.

title: Supraventricular tachycardia – Acute management: treatment if vagal manoeuvres and adenosine fail
content: If vagal manoeuvres and adenosine are ineffective, intravenous verapamil or beta-blockers should be administered.

title: Supraventricular tachycardia – Acute management: electrical cardioversion
content: Electrical cardioversion is indicated if pharmacological and vagal manoeuvres fail to terminate SVT.

title: Supraventricular tachycardia – Prevention: beta-blockers
content: Beta-blockers can be used to prevent recurrent episodes of SVT.

title: Supraventricular tachycardia – Prevention: radio-frequency ablation
content: Radio-frequency ablation is an effective preventive treatment for recurrent SVT episodes.

title: Takayasu's arteritis – Definition
content: Takayasu's arteritis is a large vessel vasculitis primarily affecting the aorta and its major branches.

title: Takayasu's arteritis – Epidemiology
content: Takayasu's arteritis is more common in younger females aged 10-40 years and in Asian populations.

title: Takayasu's arteritis – Pathophysiology
content: Takayasu's arteritis causes occlusion of the aorta and its major branches leading to ischemia and absent limb pulses.

title: Takayasu's arteritis – Systemic features
content: Systemic features include malaise and headache due to underlying vasculitis.

title: Takayasu's arteritis – Unequal blood pressure in upper limbs
content: Patients may present with unequal blood pressure measurements between the upper limbs.

title: Takayasu's arteritis – Carotid bruit and tenderness
content: Carotid artery bruit and tenderness may be present on clinical examination.

title: Takayasu's arteritis – Absent or weak peripheral pulses
content: Peripheral pulses may be absent or weak due to arterial occlusion.

title: Takayasu's arteritis – Limb claudication on exertion
content: Patients experience claudication in upper and lower limbs during exertion due to ischemia.

title: Takayasu's arteritis – Aortic regurgitation
content: Aortic regurgitation occurs in approximately 20% of patients due to aortic root involvement.

title: Takayasu's arteritis – Association with renal artery stenosis
content: Takayasu's arteritis is associated with renal artery stenosis due to involvement of renal arteries.

title: Takayasu's arteritis – Diagnostic investigations
content: Diagnosis requires vascular imaging of the arterial tree using magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) or computed tomography angiography (CTA).

title: Takayasu's arteritis – Management
content: First-line treatment for Takayasu's arteritis is corticosteroids to reduce vascular inflammation.

title: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy – Definition
content: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is a type of non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy characterized by transient apical ballooning of the myocardium.

title: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy – Trigger
content: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy may be triggered by physical or emotional stress.

title: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy – Pathophysiology description
content: The term 'Takotsubo' refers to a Japanese octopus trap, reflecting the heart's apical ballooning appearance in this condition.

title: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy – Pathophysiology mechanism
content: Apical ballooning occurs due to severe hypokinesis of the mid and apical myocardial segments with preserved contraction of the basal segments.

title: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy – Clinical presentation chest pain
content: Patients with Takotsubo cardiomyopathy commonly present with chest pain.

title: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy – Clinical presentation heart failure features
content: Patients may exhibit features of heart failure during Takotsubo cardiomyopathy.

title: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy – ECG findings
content: Electrocardiogram typically shows ST-segment elevation in Takotsubo cardiomyopathy.

title: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy – Coronary angiogram findings
content: Coronary angiogram is typically normal in Takotsubo cardiomyopathy despite ECG changes.

title: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy – Treatment
content: Management of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is primarily supportive.

title: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy – Prognosis
content: The majority of patients with Takotsubo cardiomyopathy improve with supportive treatment.

title: Thrombolysis – Definition
content: Thrombolysis involves the use of thrombolytic drugs that act as tissue plasminogen activators, converting plasminogen into plasmin, an enzyme that breaks down fibrin and dissolves blood clots.

title: Thrombolysis – Primary Indication
content: Thrombolytic drugs are primarily used in patients presenting with ST elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI).

title: Thrombolysis – Other Indications
content: Other indications for thrombolysis include acute ischaemic stroke and pulmonary embolism, although strict inclusion criteria apply.

title: Thrombolysis – Examples of Drugs
content: Examples of thrombolytic drugs include alteplase, tenecteplase, and streptokinase.

title: Thrombolysis – Contraindication: Active Internal Bleeding
content: Active internal bleeding is a contraindication to thrombolysis due to increased risk of hemorrhage.

title: Thrombolysis – Contraindication: Recent Haemorrhage, Trauma or Surgery
content: Recent haemorrhage, trauma, or surgery, including dental extraction, contraindicates thrombolysis due to bleeding risk.

title: Thrombolysis – Contraindication: Coagulation and Bleeding Disorders
content: Coagulation and bleeding disorders are contraindications to thrombolysis due to elevated hemorrhage risk.

title: Thrombolysis – Contraindication: Intracranial Neoplasm
content: Presence of an intracranial neoplasm contraindicates thrombolysis because of increased bleeding risk.

title: Thrombolysis – Contraindication: Stroke Within 3 Months
content: A history of stroke within the previous 3 months is a contraindication to thrombolysis due to hemorrhagic risk.

title: Thrombolysis – Contraindication: Aortic Dissection
content: Aortic dissection is a contraindication to thrombolysis because it may worsen bleeding and dissection.

title: Thrombolysis – Contraindication: Recent Head Injury
content: Recent head injury contraindicates thrombolysis due to increased risk of intracranial hemorrhage.

title: Thrombolysis – Contraindication: Severe Hypertension
content: Severe hypertension is a contraindication to thrombolysis due to increased risk of hemorrhagic complications.

title: Thrombolysis – Side Effect: Haemorrhage
content: Haemorrhage is a common side effect of thrombolytic therapy due to fibrin breakdown and impaired clotting.

title: Thrombolysis – Side Effect: Hypotension
content: Hypotension is a side effect of thrombolysis and is more commonly observed with streptokinase.

title: Thrombolysis – Side Effect: Allergic Reactions with Streptokinase
content: Allergic reactions may occur with streptokinase administration during thrombolytic therapy.

title: Torsades de pointes – Definition
content: Torsades de pointes is a form of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia associated with a long QT interval.

title: Torsades de pointes – Pathophysiology
content: Torsades de pointes may deteriorate into ventricular fibrillation, which can lead to sudden death.

title: Long QT interval – Congenital causes
content: Congenital causes of long QT interval include Jervell-Lange-Nielsen syndrome and Romano-Ward syndrome.

title: Long QT interval – Drug-induced causes
content: Drugs that can cause long QT interval include antiarrhythmics such as amiodarone, sotalol, class 1a antiarrhythmic drugs, tricyclic antidepressants, antipsychotics, chloroquine, terfenadine, and erythromycin.

title: Long QT interval – Electrolyte causes
content: Electrolyte abnormalities causing long QT interval include hypocalcaemia, hypokalaemia, and hypomagnesaemia.

title: Long QT interval – Other medical causes
content: Other medical causes of long QT interval include myocarditis, hypothermia, and subarachnoid haemorrhage.

title: Torsades de pointes – Management
content: Intravenous magnesium sulphate is the treatment of choice for torsades de pointes.

title: Travel-related thrombosis – Definition
content: Travel-related thrombosis refers to venous thromboembolism (VTE) occurring in association with prolonged travel, especially long-haul flights.

title: Travel-related thrombosis – Pathophysiology of risk in long-haul flights
content: Long-haul air travel is associated with increased risk of venous thromboembolism due to prolonged immobility leading to venous stasis and hypercoagulability.

title: Travel-related thrombosis – Risk of pulmonary embolism by travel distance
content: Pulmonary embolism risk increases with travel distance: 0.01 cases per million for travel under 5,000 km, 1.5 cases per million for 5,000-10,000 km, and 4.8 cases per million for travel over 10,000 km.

title: Travel-related thrombosis – Guidelines on prevention from British Committee for Standards in Haematology and SIGN
content: British Committee for Standards in Haematology (2005) and SIGN (2010) published guidelines on prevention of travel-related thrombosis, but no universal consensus exists.

title: Travel-related thrombosis – Role of Civil Aviation Authority guidance
content: The Civil Aviation Authority does not provide specific guidance regarding venous thromboembolism prevention in air travel.

title: Travel-related thrombosis – Use of anti-embolism stockings in major risk patients
content: Patients with major risk factors for travel-related thrombosis should consider wearing anti-embolism stockings, which can be purchased or prescribed (class I recommendation).
