title: Travel-related thrombosis – Management of very high risk patients
content: For very high risk patients (e.g., long-haul flight after recent major surgery), delaying the flight or seeking specialist advice regarding low-molecular weight heparin use should be considered.

title: Travel-related thrombosis – Role of aspirin in prevention
content: All guidelines agree that aspirin has no role in preventing travel-related thrombosis in low, medium, or high risk patients.

title: Tricuspid regurgitation – Definition
content: Tricuspid regurgitation is a condition characterized by the backflow of blood from the right ventricle into the right atrium during systole due to incompetence of the tricuspid valve.

title: Tricuspid regurgitation – Sign: Pan-systolic murmur
content: A pan-systolic murmur is a continuous heart murmur heard throughout systole, commonly associated with tricuspid regurgitation.

title: Tricuspid regurgitation – Sign: Prominent/giant V waves in jugular venous pressure
content: Prominent or giant V waves in the jugular venous pressure waveform indicate increased right atrial pressure during ventricular systole, commonly seen in tricuspid regurgitation.

title: Tricuspid regurgitation – Sign: Pulsatile hepatomegaly
content: Pulsatile hepatomegaly is an enlarged liver with a palpable pulsation due to transmitted venous pulsations from tricuspid regurgitation.

title: Tricuspid regurgitation – Sign: Left parasternal heave
content: A left parasternal heave is a palpable precordial impulse due to right ventricular hypertrophy, which can be present in tricuspid regurgitation.

title: Tricuspid regurgitation – Cause: Right ventricular infarction
content: Right ventricular infarction can cause tricuspid regurgitation by impairing right ventricular function and tricuspid valve competence.

title: Tricuspid regurgitation – Cause: Pulmonary hypertension
content: Pulmonary hypertension, such as that caused by chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), can lead to tricuspid regurgitation by causing right ventricular pressure overload and valve incompetence.

title: Tricuspid regurgitation – Cause: Rheumatic heart disease
content: Rheumatic heart disease can cause tricuspid regurgitation through valvular damage and scarring affecting the tricuspid valve.

title: Tricuspid regurgitation – Cause: Infective endocarditis
content: Infective endocarditis, especially in intravenous drug users, can cause tricuspid regurgitation by damaging the tricuspid valve leaflets.

title: Tricuspid regurgitation – Cause: Ebstein's anomaly
content: Ebstein's anomaly is a congenital malformation of the tricuspid valve that can cause tricuspid regurgitation due to leaflet displacement and malformation.

title: Tricuspid regurgitation – Cause: Carcinoid syndrome
content: Carcinoid syndrome can cause tricuspid regurgitation by inducing fibrous plaque formation on the tricuspid valve leaflets leading to valve dysfunction.

title: Valsalva manoeuvre – Definition
content: The Valsalva manoeuvre is a forced exhalation against a closed airway, producing four characteristic phases of blood pressure and heart rate change.

title: Valsalva manoeuvre – Baroreflex activation
content: The Valsalva manoeuvre triggers the baroreflex, a key mechanism for assessing autonomic nervous system function.

title: Valsalva manoeuvre – Clinical use in cardiology
content: Used as a bedside intervention to terminate some episodes of supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) by increasing vagal tone and as part of heart murmur assessment, including accentuation of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy and reduction of aortic stenosis murmurs.

title: Valsalva manoeuvre – Clinical use in autonomic testing
content: Used to assess baroreflex integrity and diagnose disorders of autonomic function.

title: Valsalva manoeuvre – Clinical use in ENT and aviation medicine
content: Used to equalise middle ear pressure during changes in altitude or pressure.

title: Valsalva manoeuvre – Phase I pathophysiology
content: Onset of strain with forced exhalation against closed airway increases intrathoracic and intra-abdominal pressure, compressing the aorta and large chest vessels, causing a brief spike in blood pressure and slight heart rate decrease.

title: Valsalva manoeuvre – Phase II pathophysiology
content: Continued strain maintains raised intrathoracic pressure, compressing great veins and reducing venous return, leading to decreased ventricular filling, stroke volume, and blood pressure; baroreflex triggers sympathetic activation increasing heart rate and vasoconstriction, causing partial blood pressure recovery.

title: Valsalva manoeuvre – Phase III pathophysiology
content: Release of strain causes sudden fall in intrathoracic pressure as normal breathing resumes, leading to transient changes in blood pressure and heart rate (content truncated).

title: Ventricular tachycardia – Peri-arrest broad complex tachycardia assumption
content: In a peri-arrest situation, a broad complex tachycardia should be assumed to be ventricular in origin according to the European Resuscitation Council, even though it may result from a supraventricular rhythm with aberrant conduction.

title: Ventricular tachycardia – Adverse signs indicating immediate cardioversion
content: Adverse signs in ventricular tachycardia that indicate immediate cardioversion include systolic blood pressure less than 90 mmHg, chest pain, heart failure, and syncope.

title: Ventricular tachycardia – Immediate cardioversion indication
content: Immediate cardioversion is indicated in ventricular tachycardia patients presenting with adverse signs such as hypotension, chest pain, heart failure, or syncope.

title: Ventricular tachycardia – Use of antiarrhythmics in absence of adverse signs
content: In ventricular tachycardia patients without adverse signs, antiarrhythmic drugs may be used as initial management.

title: Ventricular tachycardia – Electrical cardioversion after failed antiarrhythmics
content: If antiarrhythmic drug therapy fails to control ventricular tachycardia, electrical cardioversion with synchronized direct current shocks may be required.

title: Ventricular tachycardia – Amiodarone administration route
content: Amiodarone is ideally administered through a central line when used for ventricular tachycardia management.

title: Ventricular tachycardia – Lidocaine caution in severe left ventricular impairment
content: Lidocaine should be used with caution in ventricular tachycardia patients who have severe left ventricular impairment.

title: Ventricular tachycardia – Procainamide use
content: Procainamide is an antiarrhythmic drug option for the management of ventricular tachycardia.

title: Ventricular tachycardia – Verapamil contraindication
content: Verapamil should NOT be used in the management of ventricular tachycardia.

title: Ventricular tachycardia – Electrophysiological study after failed drug therapy
content: If drug therapy fails to control ventricular tachycardia, an electrophysiological study (EPS) may be performed for further evaluation and management.

title: Ventricular tachycardia – Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator indication
content: Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) placement is particularly indicated in ventricular tachycardia patients with significantly impaired left ventricular function.

title: Warfarin – Definition
content: Warfarin is an oral anticoagulant historically used as first-line therapy for venous thromboembolism management and stroke risk reduction in atrial fibrillation patients.

title: Warfarin – Current clinical use
content: Warfarin use has been largely superseded by direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) due to DOACs requiring less intensive monitoring.

title: Warfarin – Mechanism of action
content: Warfarin inhibits epoxide reductase, preventing the reduction of vitamin K to its active hydroquinone form, which is necessary as a cofactor for carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, X and protein C.

title: Warfarin – Indications mechanical heart valves
content: Warfarin is indicated for anticoagulation in patients with mechanical heart valves, with target INR depending on valve type and location; mitral valves generally require a higher INR than aortic valves.

title: Warfarin – Indications venous thromboembolism second-line
content: Warfarin is used as a second-line anticoagulant after DOACs for venous thromboembolism, with a target INR of 2.5, increased to 3.5 if recurrent events occur.

title: Warfarin – Indications atrial fibrillation second-line
content: Warfarin is used as a second-line anticoagulant after DOACs for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation, with a target INR of 2.5.

title: Warfarin – Monitoring with INR
content: Warfarin therapy is monitored using the international normalized ratio (INR), which is the ratio of the patient's prothrombin time to normal prothrombin time.

title: Warfarin – Pharmacokinetics and dose adjustment
content: Warfarin has a long half-life and achieving a stable INR may take several days; various loading regimens exist and computer software is often used to adjust dosing.

title: Warfarin – Factors potentiating effect
content: Warfarin effect is potentiated by liver disease, cytochrome P450 enzyme inhibitors such as amiodarone and ciprofloxacin, cranberry juice, drugs that displace warfarin from plasma albumin like NSAIDs, and drugs that inhibit platelet function such as NSAIDs.

title: Warfarin – Side effect haemorrhage
content: A major side effect of warfarin therapy is hemorrhage due to its anticoagulant effect.

title: Warfarin – Teratogenicity and breastfeeding
content: Warfarin is teratogenic and generally contraindicated in pregnancy but can be used safely in breastfeeding mothers.

title: Warfarin – Skin necrosis pathophysiology
content: Warfarin-induced skin necrosis occurs due to an initial reduction in protein C biosynthesis when starting warfarin, causing a temporary procoagulant state that may lead to venular thrombosis and skin necrosis.

title: Warfarin – Prevention of initial procoagulant state
content: The initial procoagulant state caused by warfarin-induced protein C reduction is normally avoided by concurrent administration of heparin when starting warfarin therapy.

title: Warfarin – Purple toes syndrome
content: Purple toes syndrome is a rare complication of warfarin therapy characterized by painful purple discoloration of the toes.

title: Warfarin – Interaction with Liver Disease
content: Liver disease potentiates the effect of warfarin by impairing metabolism, increasing bleeding risk.

title: Warfarin – Interaction with P450 Enzyme Inhibitors
content: P450 enzyme inhibitors increase warfarin plasma levels, leading to elevated INR and bleeding risk.

title: Warfarin – Interaction with Cranberry Juice
content: Cranberry juice potentiates warfarin effect, increasing INR and bleeding risk.

title: Warfarin – Interaction with Drugs Displacing Warfarin from Plasma Albumin
content: Drugs such as NSAIDs displace warfarin from plasma albumin, increasing free warfarin levels and bleeding risk.

title: Warfarin – Interaction with NSAIDs Inhibiting Platelet Function
content: NSAIDs inhibit platelet function, increasing bleeding risk when combined with warfarin.

title: Warfarin – Effect of P450 Enzyme Inducers on INR
content: P450 enzyme inducers decrease warfarin plasma levels, reducing INR and anticoagulant effect.

title: Warfarin – P450 Enzyme Inducers Examples
content: Examples of P450 enzyme inducers that decrease INR include phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbitone, rifampicin, St John's Wort, chronic alcohol intake, griseofulvin, and smoking.

title: Warfarin – Effect of P450 Enzyme Inhibitors on INR
content: P450 enzyme inhibitors increase warfarin plasma levels, increasing INR and bleeding risk.

title: Warfarin – P450 Enzyme Inhibitors Examples
content: Examples of P450 enzyme inhibitors that increase INR include ciprofloxacin, clarithromycin, erythromycin, isoniazid, cimetidine, omeprazole, amiodarone, allopurinol, ketoconazole, fluconazole, fluoxetine, sertraline, ritonavir, sodium valproate, acute alcohol intake, and quinupristin.

title: Warfarin – Management of major bleeding with high INR
content: In cases of major bleeding such as variceal haemorrhage or intracranial haemorrhage in patients on warfarin, warfarin should be stopped immediately. Administer intravenous vitamin K 5 mg. Use prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) for rapid reversal; if PCC is unavailable, fresh frozen plasma (FFP) may be used, though it takes longer to prepare.

title: Warfarin – Management of INR >8.0 with minor bleeding
content: For patients on warfarin with INR greater than 8.0 and minor bleeding, stop warfarin and give intravenous vitamin K 1-3 mg. Repeat vitamin K dose if INR remains elevated after 24 hours. Restart warfarin when INR is less than 5.0.

title: Warfarin – Management of INR >8.0 without bleeding
content: In patients on warfarin with INR greater than 8.0 but no bleeding, stop warfarin and give oral vitamin K 1-5 mg using the intravenous preparation administered orally. Repeat vitamin K dose if INR remains elevated after 24 hours. Restart warfarin when INR is less than 5.0.

title: Warfarin – Management of INR 5.0-8.0 with minor bleeding
content: For patients on warfarin with INR between 5.0 and 8.0 and minor bleeding, stop warfarin and give intravenous vitamin K 1-3 mg. Restart warfarin when INR is less than 5.0.

title: Warfarin – Management of INR 5.0-8.0 without bleeding
content: In patients on warfarin with INR between 5.0 and 8.0 and no bleeding, withhold one or two doses of warfarin and reduce the subsequent maintenance dose.

title: Prothrombin complex concentrate – Use in intracranial haemorrhage with warfarin
content: Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) should be considered for rapid reversal of warfarin anticoagulation in cases of intracranial haemorrhage because fresh frozen plasma (FFP) requires time to defrost and prepare.

title: Wolff-Parkinson White – Definition
content: Wolff-Parkinson White (WPW) syndrome is caused by a congenital accessory conducting pathway between the atria and ventricles leading to atrioventricular re-entry tachycardia (AVRT).

title: Wolff-Parkinson White – Pathophysiology of Accessory Pathway
content: The accessory pathway in WPW syndrome does not slow conduction, allowing atrial fibrillation (AF) to rapidly degenerate into ventricular fibrillation (VF).

title: Wolff-Parkinson White – Typical Age of Presentation
content: WPW syndrome typically presents in teenagers and young adults but can occur at any age.

title: Wolff-Parkinson White – Palpitations Presentation
content: Patients with WPW syndrome commonly present with palpitations characterized by sudden onset and offset, often rapid and regular.

title: Wolff-Parkinson White – Light-headedness and Pre-syncope Presentation
content: Light-headedness and pre-syncope are possible presenting symptoms in WPW syndrome.

title: Wolff-Parkinson White – ECG Feature: Short PR Interval
content: A short PR interval is a possible electrocardiogram (ECG) feature in WPW syndrome.

title: Wolff-Parkinson White – ECG Feature: Wide QRS Complexes with Delta Wave
content: WPW syndrome ECG may show wide QRS complexes with a slurred upstroke known as a 'delta wave'.

title: Wolff-Parkinson White – ECG Feature: Left Axis Deviation with Right-sided Accessory Pathway
content: Left axis deviation on ECG is seen in the majority of WPW cases and is associated with a right-sided accessory pathway.

title: Wolff-Parkinson White – ECG Feature: Right Axis Deviation with Left-sided Accessory Pathway
content: Right axis deviation on ECG is associated with a left-sided accessory pathway in WPW syndrome.

title: Wolff-Parkinson White – Differentiation of Type A and Type B
content: Type A WPW (left-sided pathway) shows a dominant R wave in lead V1, whereas type B WPW (right-sided pathway) does not have a dominant R wave in V1.

title: Wolff-Parkinson White – Associations: Hypertrophic Obstructive Cardiomyopathy
content: WPW syndrome is associated with hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM).

title: Wolff-Parkinson White – Associations: Mitral Valve Prolapse
content: WPW syndrome is associated with mitral valve prolapse.

title: Wolff-Parkinson White – Associations: Ebstein's Anomaly
content: WPW syndrome is associated with Ebstein's anomaly.

title: Wolff-Parkinson White – Associations: Thyrotoxicosis
content: WPW syndrome is associated with thyrotoxicosis.

title: Wolff-Parkinson White – Associations: Secundum Atrial Septal Defect
content: WPW syndrome is associated with secundum atrial septal defect (ASD).

title: Wolff-Parkinson White – Definitive Treatment
content: The definitive treatment for WPW syndrome is radiofrequency ablation of the accessory pathway.

title: Wolff-Parkinson White – Medical Therapy Options
content: Medical therapy options for WPW syndrome include sotalol, amiodarone, and flecainide.

title: Wolff-Parkinson White – Sotalol Contraindication in Atrial Fibrillation
content: Sotalol should be avoided in WPW patients with coexistent atrial fibrillation because prolonging the AV node refractory period may increase conduction through the accessory pathway, raising ventricular rate and risking ventricular fibrillation.
